Speaking together in time: An investigation of prosodic timing structure and unison production in people with aphasia

## Abstract

Aphasia is an acquired language disorder, typically resulting from stroke, that can affect

the ability to speak fluently and accurately. Many effective treatments to improve spoken language

production in persons with aphasia (PWAs) involve unison production, in which the PWA speaks

along with a clinician or recording. However, the mechanism underlying this technique is not well

understood. To maximize therapeutic efficiency of unison production, it is critical to understand

how it works, and which types of stimuli are most effective.

One key variable that differs across unison production approaches is the prosodic timing

structure—the patterning of stressed versus unstressed syllables within the stimulus phrases.

Most approaches use a “conversational,” syntax-influenced timing structure, while others,

particularly music-based treatments, use a beat-based, “metrical” timing structure. Recent

research has shown that beat-based rhythm can particularly benefit spoken output in PWAs,

suggesting that it may promote entrainment to the stimulus, i.e., using temporal prediction to guide

planning and subsequent production of speech in unison with the model. This dissertation

investigates this idea by comparing conversational versus metrical prosodic timing structure

during unison production on PWAs’ (a) syllable production accuracy, and (b) timing alignment

with the unison stimulus—an objective measure of temporal prediction and stability.

In Study 1, group-level comparisons reveal that speaking along with metrically timed

stimuli yields (a) a higher percentage of accurate syllables, particularly for individuals with the

nonfluent aphasia subtype, and (b) earlier and less variable timing alignment, suggesting

enhanced temporal prediction. Study 2 employs item-level regression analyses to explore

whether stressed syllables, which are typically more acoustically and linguistically salient than

unstressed syllables, are more likely to be produced accurately and/or show evidence of

Overall, results suggest that prosodic timing structure should be considered when

designing unison production stimuli, as metrical timing facilitates entrainment, leading to more

accurate spoken output among PWAs.

## Chapter 1: Introduction


<!-- Page 20 -->


2

Aphasia is an acquired communication disability, typically due to stroke, that affects an

estimated two million people in the United States (National Aphasia Association, n.d.). Aphasia

affects the ability to produce and comprehend language, and is often broadly classified into

subtypes based on how these abilities are impacted (American Speech-Language-Hearing

Association [ASHA], n.d.). Individuals with “nonfluent” subtypes of aphasia exhibit difficulty

formulating grammatical sentences (agrammatism), recalling words (anomia), and may also have

concomitant apraxia of speech (AOS), a motor speech disorder that affects the planning and

sequencing of speech sounds (ASHA, n.d.; National Institute on Deafness and Other

Communication Disorders [NIDCD], 2015). Treatment for aphasia and AOS consists of

compensatory practices, focused on using alternative strategies to enable communication

access, and restorative practices, designed to directly rehabilitate language and speech abilities.

This dissertation examines unison production, a technique incorporated into many

restorative treatment approaches for nonfluent aphasia, in which the person with aphasia (PWA)

speaks words or phrases aloud with a clinician or recording (Albert et al., 1973; Cherney et al.,

1986; Lee et al., 2009; Norton et al., 2009; Rosenbek & Wertz, 1972). Unison production can

have a striking, immediate effect for many PWAs, including those with severe aphasia who have

limited independent spoken output: When asked to “say it with me,” words and phrases are often

produced more accurately and fluently than when attempted alone. Evidence for the benefit of

unison production has been demonstrated in well-controlled studies, revealing that compared to

solo production, speaking in unison yields productions that are more accurate (Kershenbaum et

al., 2019; Racette et al., 2006) and contain a greater diversity of overall words produced

(Fridriksson et al., 2012). Additionally, studies of treatments that incorporate unison production

have revealed improvements in the fluency of PWAs’ independent spoken output, suggesting that

this technique may aid both linguistic and motor planning aspects of production (Cherney, 2010;

Lee et al., 2009; Zumbansen et al., 2014b).


<!-- Page 21 -->


3

While unison production appears to facilitate spoken output in PWAs, the mechanism by

which it works is not well understood. As a result, different ways of implementing unison

production have resulted in substantial heterogeneity across study designs and treatment

protocols, limiting current understanding of the factors that predict success with this technique.

One key difference across studies and treatments is the prosodic timing structure of the stimuli

used during unison production. Prosodic timing structure refers to the timing and duration of

sounds and silences within an utterance—including the patterning of stressed (i.e., “prominent”

or “emphasized”) syllables versus unstressed words and syllables. Unison production studies and

treatments can be divided into two categories according to this particular aspect of prosodic timing

structure. Most use a “conversational” timing structure, akin to natural, everyday prosody, in which

the location  of prominent, “stressed” syllables in the phrase is influenced by the underlying syntax

(Watson & Gibson, 2004, 2005) and information structure (Pierrehumbert & Hirschberg, 2003;

Terken & Nooteboom, 1987) of the spoken sentence. On the other hand, music-based treatments,

such as melodic intonation therapy, use beat-based, “metrical” prosodic timing, in which stressed

syllables occur in rhythmically regular patterns across the sentence, similar to metered poetry

(Albert et al., 1973; Norton et al., 2009; Stahl et al., 2013).

In current practice, prosodic timing structure is not typically taken into account when

determining unison treatment targets. However, a growing body of work has suggested that

metrical timing may be particularly beneficial for PWAs, whether via singing (Racette et al., 2006)

or speaking along with rhythmically regular stimuli (Aichert et al., 2019; Kershenbaum et al., 2019;

Stahl et al., 2011). Aside from the prosodic timing of the stimuli themselves, the use of metrical

timing to facilitate spoken output has been explored via speaking along with external metronomes

(Dworkin et al., 1988; Mauszycki & Wambaugh, 2008; Quique et al., 2022; Wambaugh &

Martinez, 2000), as well as with rhythmic hand tapping—another notable component of melodic

intonation therapy (Curtis et al., 2020; Norton et al., 2009). Furthermore, among people without

aphasia, metrical timing has been shown to protect against speech errors during nonword


<!-- Page 22 -->


4

repetition, indicating a production advantage of rhythmic regularity even within an intact language

system (Tilsen, 2011). Thus, while multiple sources of evidence indicate that (1) unison production

is beneficial for PWAs and (2) metrical timing may aid spoken production, there has not been a

direct comparison of conversational versus metrical prosodic timing during unison production in

PWAs.

This dissertation therefore explicitly examines prosodic timing structure as a potentially

critical stimulus variable that can enhance the beneficial effects of unison production for PWAs.

As part of this investigation, we also evaluate entrainment as the underlying mechanism by which

unison production works. Entrainment refers to the synchronization of one’s actions in time with

an external stimulus—an ability made possible by predicting the timing of upcoming events in that

stimulus (Beier & Ferreira, 2018; Cummins, 2009; Phillips-Silver et al., 2010; Thaut et al., 2015).

When speaking along with conversationally timed stimuli, it is possible to anticipate the timing of

upcoming material on the basis of linguistic structure (Cummins, 2009; Cutler, 1976). However,

metrically timed stimuli are more rhythmically regular, which can facilitate prediction by providing

a “stable anticipatory template” (Thaut et al., 2015, p. 2) that is not reliant on linguistic

processing—a factor that which may be particularly beneficial for people with nonfluent aphasia.

In short, speaking along with a more temporally predictable prosodic structure can lessen the

linguistic processing load, freeing up resources that can be allocated to other aspects of spoken

language production. This in turn can lead to improved accuracy and fluency of spoken output—

an idea discussed more thoroughly in the introduction to Chapter 2. Thus, in addition to examining

the effects of prosodic timing structure on accuracy of spoken output, this work also examines

whether entrainment is enhanced by metrical timing, quantified by measuring the timing alignment

between PWAs’ spoken productions and the unison model.

The questions raised thus far regarding prosodic timing structure are concerned with how

the overall patterning of stressed versus unstressed syllables in each prosodic timing framework

might affect accuracy and entrainment. Building on this idea, the second study reported in this


<!-- Page 23 -->


5

dissertation (Chapter 3) “zooms in” further to the level of the individual syllable, exploring whether

the facilitating effects of unison production and metrical timing benefit prediction and production

of all syllables, or just the emphasized, stressed syllables, which are more acoustically and

prosodically salient (e.g., Cole et al., 2019), and have been described as “islands of reliability”

that may help listeners allocate attention in time during language processing (Pitt & Samuel,

1990). Multiple non-unison studies have suggested that in certain linguistic contexts, stressed

syllables may be less vulnerable to error or omission during production by PWAs (Goodglass et

al., 2001; Howard & Smith, 2002; Nickels & Howard, 1999) and people without aphasia (Croot et

al., 2010; Kember et al., 2017). In addition, psycholinguistic perception studies have found

processing advantages for syllables that are temporally predicted to be stressed based on the

surrounding prosodic context (see review by Beier & Ferreira, 2018, and references therein).

Thus, it is logical to ask whether the benefits associated with unison production and/or

metrical timing are specifically driven by amplifying the privileged status of stressed syllables, or

alternatively, whether these facilitating contexts serve to “even the playing field” by aiding

prediction/production of unstressed syllables as well. By exploring how unison production,

metrical timing, and phrasal stress contribute (individually and in combination) to production

accuracy and temporal prediction, we can gain a better understanding of the underlying

mechanism of unison production. This in turn can inform unison production treatment approaches

by providing insight into how to optimize the design of stimulus phrases based on these variables.

Dissertation structure

This dissertation is structured as follows: Chapter 2 provides an in-depth review of extant

literature regarding unison production treatment approaches for aphasia, metrical timing, and

definitions of entrainment. It continues with a study reporting the effect of metrical versus

conversational prosodic timing on (1) the percentage of accurately produced syllables and (2)

participant-stimulus timing alignment (a proxy for temporal prediction, measured in the speech

signal) during unison production. Chapter 3 builds upon these analyses in an expanded data set

by examining both accuracy and unison timing alignment of stressed versus unstressed syllables

in metrical versus conversational timing structures. The specific research questions addressed in

Chapters 2 and 3 are outlined in Table 1.1. Finally, Chapter 4 provides a general discussion

synthesizing key findings, describing clinical implications, and offering directions for future

research.

Chapter 2 The effect of prosodic timing structure on unison production in people with aphasia

Aim 1: Establish the overall effect of unison production vs. solo repetition on accuracy of spoken output. Hypothesis: Unison production will yield a greater % of accurate syllables compared to solo production.

Aim 2: Compare the effect of metrical vs. conversational timing structure on accuracy of spoken output during unison production. Hypothesis: Metrical timing will yield a greater % of accurate syllables compared to conversational timing.

Aim 3: Investigate whether entrainment is a possible mechanism of unison production by comparing the timing alignment between participant spoken productions and the unison model in each prosodic timing framework

Hypothesis: Compared to conversational timing, the enhanced temporal prediction afforded by metrical timing will yield productions that occur earlier in time and are less variable in their alignment with the unison model.

Aim 4: Provide preliminary insight into who may benefit most from metrically based treatments by examining individual differences in performance among nonfluent versus more fluent PWAs.

Chapter 3 Stressed syllables, strong beats: An exploration of phrasal stress, metrical timing, and unison production

Significance of the research

The research described in this dissertation has the potential to inform both theory and

clinical practice regarding unison production, a common therapeutic technique used in aphasia

rehabilitation. First, by investigating the role of prosodic timing structure during unison production,

this work can determine whether metrical timing promotes more accurate spoken output. Prior

research has suggested this idea in studies comparing speech to singing, but no study has directly

compared conversational versus metrical prosodic timing in spoken contexts—and most current

unison production treatments use spoken conversational timing. Second, by quantifying the

temporal relationship between PWAs’ spoken output and the unison stimuli, this research can

evaluate whether entrainment—a predictive process that enables synchrony of one’s actions with

an external stimulus—is a candidate mechanism for unison production. Entrainment has been

described in relation to unison speech production but has not yet been empirically quantified in

the speech signal. Finally, given that the patterning of stressed versus unstressed syllables in the

stimuli may make a critical difference in enhancing unison production benefits, exploring whether

stressed and unstressed syllables are differentially affected in spoken output can provide further

insight into the mechanism of unison production, which may have implications for the design of

stimulus phrases used in clinical treatment and future research.

## Introduction

Unison production is a common treatment technique for nonfluent aphasia and/or apraxia

of speech (AOS), in which the clinician and the person with aphasia (PWA) produce phrases or

sentences aloud together. The effect can be striking, enabling individuals who have limited

independent spoken output to more fluently produce words and phrases (Albert et al., 1973;

Fridriksson et al., 2012; Kershenbaum et al., 2019; Racette et al., 2006). This observation has led

to the development of several well-established, formal treatments that incorporate unison

production as a core component, including Oral Reading for Language in Aphasia (ORLA;

Cherney, 2010; Cherney et al., 1986), script training approaches (Lee et al., 2009) , integral

stimulation for AOS (Rosenbek & Wertz, 1972), and music-based approaches such as melodic

intonation therapy (MIT; Albert et al., 1973; Norton et al., 2009). Indeed, the creators of MIT

deemed unison production one of the most “clinically facilitating” aspects of the treatment

(Zumbansen et al., 2014a).

The ultimate goal of most unison production treatments is to improve functional spoken

communication, and this has been supported by evidence from a number of treatment studies,

for example, ORLA (Cherney, 2010), script training (Lee et al., 2009), and MIT (Zumbansen et

al., 2014b). In addition, experiments directly comparing repetition in unison and solo conditions

have reported more accurate production in the unison condition: Kershenbaum et al. (2019) found

that participants produced a higher percentage of accurate syllables during unison production of

both sung and spoken phrases. Racette et al. (2006) reported similar findings, measured in

percentage of words correctly produced. A number of studies have shown that nonfluent PWAs

specifically exhibit greater benefit from unison production than fluent PWAs (Fridriksson et al.,

2012, 2015; Kershenbaum et al., 2019), which aligns with the clinical intuition that nonfluent PWAs

are typically considered to be ideal candidates for treatments incorporating unison production

(e.g., Norton et al., 2009). However, the facilitatory effects of unison speech have also been

reported in other populations, including people who stutter (Andrews et al., 1982; Juste et al.,

2018; Kiefte & Armson, 2008; Ritto et al., 2016) and individuals with Parkinson’s disease (Juste

et al., 2018). Thus, unison production appears to be a useful technique for supporting fluency and

accuracy of spoken output across several populations, but the factors that influence its efficacy

remain largely unknown.

The significance of prosodic timing structure

Prosodic timing structure refers to the durational patterns of sounds and silent pauses

over the course of a phrase or sentence. In everyday “conversational” speech, the timing structure

of a spoken utterance is influenced by a number of interrelated factors across linguistic domains.

For example, lexically stressed syllables are typically longer in duration than their unstressed

counterparts (e.g., “CON-duct” vs. “con-DUCT”; e.g., Klatt, 1976), as are prominent, stressed

syllables in words that are “emphasized” by the speaker to convey information structure (e.g., “I’d

like a GREEN apple, not a red one.”; e.g., Klatt, 1976) . Syllables that occur just prior to phrase

boundaries are also often longer in duration than preceding syllables—a phenomenon known as

phrase-final lengthening (Klatt, 1976; see also Turk & Shattuck-Hufnagel, 2020). Thus, the

planning and production of the prosodic timing structure of an utterance relies on the integration

of lexical, syntactic, and pragmatic aspects of language, as well as motor planning and execution

processes.

Prosodic timing structure is also a key variable that differs across unison production

therapy approaches for PWAs. Most approaches are implemented with prosody akin to the

natural, “conversational” speech described above, in which the location and realization of

prominent, “emphasized” words and phrase boundaries are influenced by underlying syntactic

structure (Watson & Gibson, 2004, 2005) and information structure (Pierrehumbert & Hirschberg,

2003; Terken & Nooteboom, 1987). In contrast, music and rhythm-based approaches frequently

employ a beat-based “metrical” timing structure, in which prominent syllables occur in rhythmically

12

regular patterns and durations throughout the stimulus sentence, as is often the case in poetry

and song (Albert et al., 1973; Norton et al., 2009; Stahl et al., 2013).

These two prosodically contrasting approaches to unison production have not been

empirically compared in PWAs. However, the difference between them may contribute in part to

conflicting results across extant studies. In an experiment using conversationally timed stimuli,

Fridriksson et al. (2012) found that unison production improved speech accuracy only when the

stimuli were presented in an audiovisual format such that the PWAs could see the other speaker’s

mouth. Auditory-only unison production had no significant effect, yielding comparable accuracy

with the PWAs’ spontaneous, solo production. The authors therefore concluded that visual input

is essential for unison production to benefit PWAs (Fridriksson et al., 2012). Yet, other studies

that employed metrically timed stimuli have demonstrated a beneficial effect of unison production

even in auditory-only conditions. Kershenbaum et al. (2019) used sung and rhythmically spoken

stimuli (both of which adhere to a metrical timing framework) and found that PWAs produced a

greater number of accurate syllables when speaking or singing in unison with audio-recorded

stimuli, rather than repeating solo. Racette et al. (2006) also used auditory-only stimuli and found

an overall benefit of unison production, with singing in unison (i.e., adhering to metrical timing)

even more effective than conversationally timed unison speech. In a unison script training study,

Quique et al. (2022) used auditorily presented sentences (with accompanying static illustrations,

i.e., not video of facial movements) and found that PWAs could successfully learn the scripted

sentences in this format and that their learning was enhanced by the addition of rhythmic beats

digitally added to the audio signal. Similarly, Stahl et al. (2011) found that auditory-only unison

speech was produced more accurately when time-aligned to a metronome than when displaced

in time from the metronome. Thus, explicit inclusion of metrical structure in the speech stimuli

may support PWAs during unison production to the extent that visual input is not required to yield

beneficial effects.

Metrical timing structure and language processing

In this article, we define metrical timing structure as the regular patterning of “strong” (S)

and “weak” (w) events, such as beats in music or syllables in spoken language. In the music

cognition literature, it has long been described that metrical structure enables participants to

generate expectancies about the temporal organization of musical events, which gives rise to the

perception of a beat, and the ability to synchronize to it (e.g., Large & Jones, 1999). In everyday

conversational language, prominent (stressed) versus nonprominent (unstressed) syllables do

not typically occur in metrically regular patterns (Lehiste, 1977). However, spoken utterances can

be produced with metrically regular patterns, and a number of studies with neurotypical individuals

have revealed processing advantages for metrically structured speech. In an event-related

potential study, Rothermich et al. (2012) embedded semantically unpredictable target words in

metrical versus nonmetrical (“irregular”) sentences and found reduced N400 amplitudes in the

metrical contexts, suggesting that metrically regular patterns facilitated the “lexico-semantic

integration” (p. 241) of the targets by increasing the predictability of their temporal occurrence.

Pitt and Samuel (1990) used neutrally stressed bisyllabic words embedded within sequences of

either S-w (iambic) or w-S (trochaic) words and found that listeners were faster at detecting target

phonemes in the syllables predicted to be stressed based on the surrounding metrical pattern.

These studies provide support for the attentional bounce hypothesis (Pitt & Samuel, 1990), which

proposes that listeners use predictions about syllabic stress patterns to focus attention during

speech perception. Quené and Port (2005) conducted a similar phoneme detection experiment,

controlling specifically for timing duration between successive stressed syllables. They found

faster detection of target phonemes in stressed syllables that occurred in isochronous versus

jittered timing intervals. The authors interpret these findings as support for dynamic attending

theory (Large & Jones, 1999), which like the attentional bounce hypothesis, proposes that

listeners allocate attention based on predictions of temporal events. However, dynamic attending


<!-- Page 32 -->


14

theory specifies a neural mechanism, proposing that individuals form expectations about when

temporal events will occur based on the synchronization of their own neural oscillations with a

temporally regular external stimulus. (For a more comprehensive discussion of temporal

prediction and stress patterns within speech perception, see review by Beier & Ferreira, 2018).

While these perception studies investigate the effect of metrical structure in different ways, the

findings broadly converge on the idea that metrical regularity aids prediction in speech perception.

Compared to perception studies, there is relatively little research explicitly investigating

the effect of metrical regularity on speech production in neurotypical individuals. Tilsen (2011)

conducted a production experiment in which participants read, silently rehearsed, and then

produced sequences of trisyllabic nonwords that were either metrically regular (i.e., all S-w-w) or

irregular (i.e., composed of both S-w-w and w-S-w). Sequences of metrically regular nonwords

were produced more quickly and with fewer errors, which the author attributed to stronger

activation and less interference among words in working memory storage, leading to faster and

more accurate planning and execution processes.

In research involving PWAs, a number of studies have explored the effects of metrical

techniques on spoken output. Multiple single-subject treatment studies have employed

metronomes and/or hand tapping for rate and rhythm control in individuals with both aphasia and

AOS, revealing positive effects on sound production accuracy (Dworkin et al., 1988; Mauszycki &

Wambaugh, 2008; Wambaugh & Martinez, 2000). Authors of these studies suggested that use of

a metronome may simply reduce overall rate to allow more time for motor planning (Mauszycki &

Wambaugh, 2008) or may serve as a cycling cue to focus the speaker’s attention on speech

initiation and precision (Dworkin et al., 1988). Hand tapping, which is notably also a key

component of MIT (Norton et al., 2009), has also been hypothesized to potentially aid PWAs in

generating an internal rhythmic framework to self-cue speech production timing (Norton et al.,

2009; Wambaugh & Martinez, 2000).

Outside of treatment studies, other research with PWAs has also described facilitating

effects of metrical timing. Several unison production studies described in the prior section found

that production accuracy was better under metrical timing conditions, such as singing (Racette et

al., 2006) or via the addition of speech-external metrical beats in the model recordings (Quique

et al., 2022; Stahl et al., 2011). In a sentence completion task, Aichert et al. (2019) found that

individuals with AOS and aphasia produced sentence-final target words more accurately when

the sentence context was metrically regular and particularly when the target word matched the

preceding metrical context (i.e., trochaic targets ending trochaic sentences). In their discussion,

they note that their participants “exploit[ed] the rhythmic cues in speech for the initiation and

segmental realization of target words” (Aichert et al., 2019, p. 3114) and suggest that the metrical

regularity of their stimuli aided participants in “generating temporal predictions and freeing

attentional resources that allowed for more correct speech production” (p. 3114). Thus, as in the

perception studies, a diverse set of approaches have revealed beneficial effects of metrical

structure on spoken output. Differences in interpretation might stem from differences in stimulus

presentation (e.g., rehearsing read words vs. listening to spoken sentences). As unison

production involves both perception and production of spoken language, it follows that the

enhanced temporal predictability afforded by metrical stimuli may confer downstream effects to

production processes, as suggested by Aichert et al.

It is worth noting that similar explanations are found in other disciplines as well. For

example, within the literature on rehabilitation of gait and extremity movements, metrical stimulus

rhythm is thought to provide a “stable anticipatory template” (Thaut et al., 2015, p. 2) that facilitates

planning and execution of motor movements. The processing benefits of a metrical timing

structure and the preference of organizing repeated behavior in a beat-based framework have

been described throughout the literature on music cognition and sensorimotor synchronization

(i.e., tapping to a beat; London, 2002; Murton et al., 2017; Repp, 2010; Repp & Su, 2013).

Determining the role of entrainment during unison production

The term “entrainment” is used in a variety of ways across disciplines, and multiple

definitions exist even just within the field of communication sciences. Some studies define it as

the natural tendency for speakers to adapt to each other’s verbal and nonverbal behaviors during

conversation (e.g., Borrie & Liss, 2014), whereas others use it as a synonym for unison speech

production (Quique et al., 2022) or as a description of the facilitating effect of speaking along with

a fluent model (Fridriksson et al., 2012). However, another definition used broadly across a

number of scientific disciplines specifies a goal of synchronous action: Entrainment is the

production of actions in time with an external stimulus (e.g., Aichert et al., 2019; Beier & Ferreira,

2018; Thaut et al., 2015). Understanding entrainment in this manner makes clear the importance

of temporal prediction. Specifically, synchronizing movements with an external stimulus depends

on (a) the extraction of timing information from that stimulus, (b) the use of that timing information

to generate expectancies (i.e., predictions) about upcoming events in the stimulus, and (c) the

use of those expectancies to guide the timing of motor output (e.g., Breska & Deouell, 2017;

Colling & Williamson, 2014). We use this latter definition of entrainment in the present study and

suggest that most unison production approaches for PWAs work by way of this type of

entrainment. Below, we outline relevant considerations for interpreting current literature on

entrainment and unison production among PWAs.

Fridriksson et al. (2012) use the term “speech entrainment” to refer to the notion that the

speech output of nonfluent PWAs is “drawn or pulled along” (p. 3816) by the fluent, unison model.

This study used conversationally timed scripts of 48-58 words in length, and participants were

instructed to “mimic” the unison model as closely as possible in real time (i.e., without prior

exposure). The authors propose that viewing the model’s mouth is critical to the success of unison

production because it provides an external framework to support the temporal coordination of

lexical processing, auditory syllable target selection, and motor planning, compensating for a


<!-- Page 35 -->


17

damaged internal “temporal gating” mechanism in PWAs (Fridriksson et al., 2012). In other words,

the authors suggest that the visual articulatory cues were necessary to aid the PWAs in predicting

upcoming words and/or movements, thereby facilitating linguistic and motor planning. This aligns

with observations made by the neurotypical controls in the Fridriksson et al. (2012) study, who

reported having to rely on predicting upcoming words when completing the audiovisual unison

task. In summary, Fridriksson et al. (2012) describe speech entrainment as a process involving

prediction that relies on visual input as an external framework to support temporal coordination of

speech planning/production processes in a disrupted system. There are some important

considerations to note regarding the ideas of prediction and timing within the Fridriksson et al.

(2012) study. The procedure differs from typical unison production approaches, especially in

therapeutic contexts, which often involve listening to the stimulus at least once before repeating

it (e.g., Cherney, 2010; Kershenbaum et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2009; Norton et al., 2009; Quique

et al., 2022; Racette et al., 2006; Stahl et al., 2011). Repetition enables participants to become

familiar with target utterances, including by extracting prosodic timing information that can guide

the timing of their own production in unison with the model. In contrast, the experimental task in

the Fridriksson et al. (2012) study requires the participant to comprehend an incoming stream of

spoken language and simultaneously make use of that information to guess upcoming words as

well as their prosodic timing in an effort to closely “speak along.” Considering that this task used

conversationally timed scripts—which are more rhythmically complex as they do not adhere to

regular, metrical timing patterns—it is not surprising that participants required multimodal input to

achieve a statistically significant performance improvement. Moreover, entrainment is

conceptualized in this study as a mimicry-based process, whereas other definitions of entrainment

(including ours) describe synchrony as a goal. Real-time mimicry is, by definition, reactive—since

the participant is perceiving the stimulus for the first time, they cannot precisely predict the timing

of unison model and therefore cannot synchronize their productions along with the unison model.


<!-- Page 36 -->


18

Thus, by our definition, participants in the Fridriksson et al. (2012) study were not in fact

“entraining” to the stimuli as much as “reacting” to them.

Prior investigations of unison speech among neurotypical individuals further highlight the

distinction between synchronous production and mimicry (also called “shadowing”) by quantifying

the temporal relationship between the speaker’s productions and the unison model stimuli.

Marslen-Wilson (1973) investigated “shadowed speech” in a real-time mimicry task similar to the

audio-only condition in the Fridriksson et al. (2012) study. In Marslen-Wilson’s study, participants’

speech consistently lagged the stimuli, with the fastest shadowers lagging at mean latencies of

250-300 ms (Marslen-Wilson, 1973). In contrast, Cummins (2002) found latencies on the order of

tens of ms when speakers practiced the material in advance through repetition (see also

Cummins, 2009, for a detailed investigation of synchronous speech and entrainment). There is a

need for more studies investigating synchronous speech, but informal comparison of these two

studies suggests that familiarity with the material can have substantial effects on speech timing.

Specifically, prior exposure to the stimuli provides the speaker with prosodic timing information in

advance, allowing for better prediction of the timing of words during unison production. This

enables lower latencies in timing alignment between the speaker’s production and the unison

model (i.e., better entrainment).

In typical unison production contexts, which involve repetition, do PWAs make use of

prosodic timing information in the stimulus to support the timing of their own production? In other

words, do PWAs “entrain” to the stimuli in unison production? Determining whether unison

production works by way of entrainment, rather than shadowing, requires investigation of the

temporal relationship between PWAs’ spoken output and the unison model used in the task. If

PWAs are entraining to stimuli during unison production, this should be observable in the timing

alignment between PWAs’ spoken output and the unison model. However, an important

consideration is that even if PWAs are entraining, they may not exhibit latencies as low as those

found in neurotypical controls (Cummins, 2002) due to disrupted linguistic and/or motor planning


<!-- Page 37 -->


19

abilities. This is where comparing contrasting prosodic timing structures becomes a useful

strategy for this investigation. As described earlier in this article, metrically timed stimuli have

rhythmically regular patterns, which we propose provide a more predictable temporal structure

that supports the planning and production of more fluent spoken output in PWAs. In other words,

rhythmic regularity within a metrically timed unison model can provide a predictable external

timing scaffold, reducing demands on the speech planning system to generate a prosodic timing

framework and freeing up more cognitive resources to allocate to other aspects of the spoken

language production process. This is in contrast to conversationally timed stimuli, which are not

rhythmically regular and may therefore depend more heavily on lexical, syntactic, and information

structure processing to guide temporal prediction during listening (Beier & Ferreira, 2018) and to

support subsequent planning and production processes. As such, while it is possible to extract

timing information from conversationally timed stimuli, and to use this temporal information to

entrain unison output with conversationally timed models, these processes are relatively more

taxing on the speaker’s language system. For PWAs, whose language abilities are disrupted,

entraining to metrically timed stimuli during unison sentence production may provide an

alternative route to more fluent, accurate spoken output. This idea aligns with both the attentional

bounce hypothesis (Pitt & Samuel, 1990), in that more regular stress patterns would enhance

prediction of upcoming material (and subsequent production), and potentially with dynamic

attending theory (Large & Jones, 1999), in that neural entrainment induced by the rhythmic

regularity of metrical stimuli may underlie the enhanced temporal prediction, enabling PWAs to

better synchronize their output with the model during unison production in this condition (see

*Figure 2.1). In fact, a phenomenon long-observed in research on motor synchronization with*

metrical stimuli is the “negative asynchrony”—that is, the tendency for individuals to produce an

action slightly ahead of the target. This phenomenon has been interpreted as further evidence of

temporal prediction, in that participants are anticipating the timing of an upcoming target (see

Aschersleben, 2002; Repp & Su, 2013, and references therein for a more complete review of this


<!-- Page 38 -->


20

work). This literature has mainly focused on finger tapping and motor movement of extremities,

and it is therefore not clear whether productions ahead of the stimulus might be observed in the

context of a unison speech task, especially for individuals with disrupted speech and language

abilities. However, we suggest that if PWAs do entrain during unison production (i.e., generate

temporal expectancies by listening to the stimuli, and use those temporal expectancies to guide

the timing of their production in an effort to synchronize with the unison model) then metrically

timed stimuli, which have a more predictable timing structure than conversationally timed stimuli,

should yield productions that (a) occur earlier in time, and (b) are less variable, reflecting more

stability in the temporal planning and production of spoken output.

Who might benefit from metrical timing?

The majority of studies investigating the use of metrical timing approaches in PWAs have

focused on persons with nonfluent aphasia (Norton et al., 2009; Racette et al., 2006; Stahl et al.,


<!-- Page 39 -->


21

2011; Wambaugh & Martinez, 2000), as this population has long been described to be ideal

candidates for such treatment techniques (Albert et al., 1973; Norton et al., 2009). Considering

the theoretical basis described above, namely, that metrical timing may provide an alternate route

to more fluent output that is less dependent on higher level linguistic processing, it makes sense

that PWAs with greater language disruption may stand to benefit the most from this approach.

However, a small number of studies have found that metrical timing can improve spoken

production among those with milder fluency impairments (Aichert et al., 2019; Mauszycki &

Wambaugh, 2008). Furthermore, given that metrical regularity has been noted to benefit spoken

language perception and production even in neurotypical individuals (see Beier & Ferreira, 2018;

Tilsen, 2011), it is somewhat surprising that research in this area to date has not included

participants with a wider range of aphasia profiles. Additionally, from a treatment perspective, it

is important to determine which clinical characteristics best predict benefit from metrically timed

stimuli in order to maximize therapeutic efficiency when prescribing and implementing such

approaches. A few studies have reported notable differences among subgroups of PWAs: Stahl

et al. (2011) found that rhythmically regular stimuli yielded more accurate spoken output

particularly among PWAs with large basal ganglia lesions. Aichert et al. (2019) found that

metrically regular sentence contexts yielded more accurate word production in both PWAs with

AOS and PWAs with phonological impairments, with severity of sound production impairment

predicting the strength of the metrical benefit. Thus, while there has been some examination of

clinical variables that might affect PWAs’ response to metrical stimuli, there is need for more

specific investigation into these factors to understand who may benefit the most from this

approach.

The present study

This preliminary study aims to investigate the effect of prosodic timing structure on the

spoken output of PWAs during unison production via four main aims: (1) to establish the overall


<!-- Page 40 -->


22

effect of unison production versus solo repetition on accuracy of spoken output (2) to compare

the effect of metrical versus conversational timing frameworks on accuracy of spoken output in

unison production in PWAs, (3) to investigate whether entrainment is a possible mechanism by

comparing the timing alignment between participant spoken productions and unison models

during each prosodic timing condition, and (4) to provide preliminary insight into who may benefit

most from metrically based treatments by examining individual differences in performance among

nonfluent versus more fluent PWAs.

Based on previous studies using a similar listen-then-repeat paradigm (Kershenbaum et

al., 2019; Racette et al., 2006), we hypothesize more accurate production in the unison condition

than in the solo condition. With regard to Aim 2, we hypothesize that the rhythmic regularity of the

metrically timed stimuli will provide a stable, predictable timing framework that frees up speech

planning and production resources, yielding more accurate spoken output than the less regular

timing structure of the conversational stimuli. For Aim 3, we hypothesize that entrainment

underlies unison production, such that the enhanced temporal prediction afforded by metrical

timing will yield productions that occur earlier in time and are less variable in their timing alignment

with the unison model, compared to conversational timing. Finally, with respect to Aim 4, we

hypothesize that individuals with nonfluent aphasia will benefit most from the predictable timing

framework output afforded by metrical timing and therefore exhibit greater and more consistent

benefits to speech accuracy and timing under metrical timing compared to more fluent PWAs.

The sentences were developed in metrical–conversational pairs to maximize phonological

Metrical sentences were recorded with a syllable rate of 2 Hz, established by using a

Data scoring: Unison timing alignment

To evaluate the timing alignment between participant productions and the stimulus model

during unison production, we extracted time points of the moment voicing began (voice onset

moment) for target syllables in both the stimulus sentences and participant productions and

compared these time points to calculate the timing offset.

Voice onset moment time points for all target syllables were extracted using the autoVOT

plugin (Keshet et al., 2014) for Praat speech analysis software (Boersma & Weenink, 2021). This

partially automated approach was chosen because it provided an efficient and reliable way to

extract acoustically salient events that are easily detectable within the speech signal and

comparable across participant productions and stimulus sentences. The autoVOT plugin has

been demonstrated to perform comparably to manual annotation even with audio from speakers

with acquired speech impairments (Buz et al., 2018) and was judged to perform reliably on an

initial sample of our data. Data from one PWA (904) were not included in the timing alignment

To set up audio files for voice onset moment identification, time intervals surrounding each

syllable onset were manually selected and labeled with the target syllable (see Figure 2.3). Each

uses a pretrained classifier to automatically detect and label the acoustic landmarks of voice onset

time (initial closure, onset of release burst, onset of voicing) in the specified search areas. (See

our comparisons, we used only the time points corresponding to the onset of voicing. Up to 64

time points (32 in each timing condition) across all sentences were extracted for each participant

and for the set of stimulus sentences.

Data analysis

All data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics, Version 26 (IBM Corp., 2019).

Nonparametric tests were conducted for all analyses. For syllable accuracy comparisons, this

conservative approach was used due to the small heterogenous sample of scores for the 15

controls and 18 PWAs, each of whom had one averaged percent accuracy score per production

condition (unison vs. solo) and timing condition (metrical vs. conversational). The same rationale

was used for timing variability comparisons, in which each participant had one SDoffset score in

each condition. For unison timing alignment comparisons, which had a larger number of data

points for each participant, a nonparametric approach was used because the data distributions

for all conditions and groups were revealed to be nonnormal by the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality

(p < .001 for all conditions and groups).

To assess whether unison production results in more accurate spoken output compared

to solo repetition (Aim 1), percentages of correct syllables in each condition were analyzed at the

group level via two Wilcoxon signed-ranks tests, separately for PWAs and controls. For this

analysis, data were collapsed across metrical and conversational timing conditions. To assess

whether metrically timed unison speech results in more accurate spoken output compared to

conversationally timed unison speech (Aim 2), we conducted a second pair of Wilcoxon signed-

ranks tests separately for PWAs and controls. While we recognize that the approach limits direct

modeling of potential interaction effects (e.g., PARTICIPANT GROUP x CONDITION or TIMING

CONDITION x PRODUCTION CONDITION), we chose this method for this preliminary investigation to

preserve statistical power and avoid Type II error. We instead compare effect sizes between

participant groups.

To evaluate whether metrical timing facilitates prediction (which would suggest

entrainment is a candidate mechanism; Aim 3), we compared timing offsets between participants’

productions and the unison stimuli in both timing conditions. For controls, central tendencies of

observations (targets produced by the same participants in metrical vs. conversational contexts).

However, we were concerned that performing a Wilcoxon signed-ranks test and discarding

## Discussion

Prior investigations of metrical timing and unison production in PWAs have compared

singing versus conversational speaking (Racette et al., 2006), added metronomic beats to spoken

stimuli (Quique et al., 2022), or tested the effect of metrical sentence contexts on single-word

production during cloze sentence tasks (Aichert et al., 2019). To our knowledge, our study is the


<!-- Page 63 -->


45

first to directly compare the effect of metrical versus conversational prosodic timing structure on

sentence-level spoken output of PWAs during unison production.

This study had four main goals. First, we aimed to establish whether PWAs produce more

accurate spoken output when speaking in unison with an auditory model versus repeating the

model “solo,” as has been found in prior, similar studies (Kershenbaum et al., 2019; Racette et

al., 2006). Then, focusing specifically on the unison condition, our second aim was to determine

whether accuracy of spoken output improves when speaking along with metrically timed versus

conversationally timed stimuli. Our third aim also focused on the unison condition. It was to

investigate the temporal alignment between participant productions and the unison stimuli in each

prosodic timing condition to determine whether there was evidence of temporal prediction (i.e.,

anticipatory timing rather than shadowing) and whether this was enhanced under metrical timing,

which is more rhythmically predictable. If so, this would support the idea that unison production

works by way of entrainment—a process of attempting to precisely synchronize one’s own output

with an external stimulus based on temporal expectancies (e.g., Cummins, 2009; Large & Jones,

1999). Our final aim was to conduct a preliminary exploration of possible performance patterns

across individual PWAs’ accuracy and timing alignment to begin to disentangle which stimulus

and clinical variables might predict benefit from metrical versus conversational timing.

PWAs produce more accurate syllables in unison versus solo repetition

Consistent with our hypothesis and with prior findings from studies with similar designs

(Kershenbaum et al., 2019; Racette et al., 2006), we found that PWAs produced a greater number

of accurate syllables overall when speaking along with an auditory model versus repeating it by

metrically timed stimuli supports the idea that prosodic timing structure can influence performance

benefit of metrical timing (Aichert et al., 2019; Kershenbaum et al., 2019; Racette et al., 2006) as

well as rhythmically enhanced stimuli (Quique et al., 2022; Stahl et al., 2011).

encoding and/or storage of word forms in working memory, leading to more accurate production

during recall, as suggested by Tilsen (2011). This interpretation would be strengthened if we also

Our third aim was to determine whether entrainment is a candidate mechanism for unison

reactively), we would expect their productions to consistently “lag” (i.e., be produced after) the

stimulus, reflecting the time required to perceive and then plan and produce the targets. Prior

research on shadowed speech, in which neurotypical participants spoke along with material they

had never heard before, has found that even the fastest shadowers still lagged the audio-recorded

consistently below 100 ms for controls. Compared to the study by Marslen-Wilson (1973), the

generally lower-latency (and in many cases, even anticipatory) timing offsets in the present study

repeating, enabling them to extract timing information that supports the subsequent planning and

production of speech in time with the unison model. Indeed, among neurotypical individuals,

similarly low timing offsets have been reported in studies of unison reading of familiar material, in

which the high degree of synchrony was attributed to entrainment, even though the material was

not metrically regular (Cummins, 2002, 2009). While methodological differences between these

prior studies and the present study may lead to slight differences in calculation of timing alignment

(e.g., accounting for line delay), the overall lower (and in many cases, anticipatory) timing offsets

mechanisms characteristic of aphasia and AOS, respectively.

An alternate interpretation of these findings is that entrainment occurs only during

metrically timed conditions and that unanticipated factors related to our study design and

measurement yielded exceptionally fast shadowing among most participants in the conversational

condition, as well as some chance productions ahead of the stimulus targets. However, we find

this explanation unlikely, as participants heard all stimuli (including conversational stimuli) twice

information based on these prior presentations, even if that timing information was more complex.

With the exception of a few participants with aphasia, the latencies found in the present study

were substantially lower than reported in prior shadowing studies (Marslen-Wilson, 1973), and

many were in fact similar to latencies described as evidence of prediction or entrainment in other

contexts (Cummins, 2002, 2009; Mates et al., 1992; Repp & Su, 2013). Furthermore, given that

PWAs by definition have difficulty with production of spoken output, it is likely that if they were

indeed shadowing in the conversational condition, they would exhibit latencies longer than those

reported for the “fastest” neurotypical shadowers, rather than latencies within the same range.

Thus, a more likely explanation is that our participants were not shadowing in either condition, but

rather using temporal prediction to guide an attempt at synchronous production of spoken output

when repeating in unison. Among most participants, this was reflected in a high degree of closely

aligned and even anticipatory timing. The rhythmic regularity of our metrical condition yielded

even less variable, more anticipatory timing, demonstrating better entrainment to the unison

model.

We remind the reader that, by our definition, metrical timing is not required for entrainment

to take place. Entrainment to conversational stimuli is possible (see Cummins, 2009) and even

potentially supported by the attentional bounce hypothesis (Pitt & Samuel, 1990), which proposes

that listeners allocate attention during speech tasks based on predictions about the occurrence

of upcoming stressed syllables but does not require that the syllables must occur in rhythmically

regular patterns. It is possible to make such predictions on the basis of other features, such as

syntax and information structure (see Beier & Ferreira, 2018), or—more likely for PWAs—other

external supports, such as written text as in ORLA (Cherney, 2010) and script training approaches

(e.g., Lee et al., 2009), or seeing the face and articulators of the unison model (Fridriksson et al.,

2012, 2015; Lee et al., 2009).

However, as is supported by work on temporal prediction and entrainment across domains

(e.g., Large & Jones, 1999; Pitt & Samuel, 1990; Thaut et al., 2015), we suggest that the rhythmic

regularity of metrical stimuli makes such prediction—and therefore entrainment—easier overall,

(Aichert et al., 2019; Kershenbaum et al., 2019; Racette et al., 2006).

Relationships between accuracy and entrainment at the individual level

As a final component of our exploratory Aim 4, we examined individual performance

patterns across all participants to determine whether individuals who speak more synchronously

with metrical unison models tend to exhibit better accuracy in this condition as well and whether

this gives rise to notable performance patterns across nonfluent and fluent subgroups of PWAs.

Nonfluent PWAs showed an apparent relationship between timing and accuracy: Of the

six nonfluent PWAs for whom we extracted timing data, five had significantly lower timing offsets

(indicating better prediction) when speaking along with metrical stimuli, and four of those five

produced a substantially greater percentage of accurate syllables in the metrical condition versus

the conversational condition (defined as score difference of ≥ 10 percentage points). This pattern

supports the idea that unison production broadly, and metrically based approaches more

specifically, are particularly well suited for nonfluent PWAs (Norton et al., 2009). We view this as

additional, more specific evidence that entrainment underlies the striking effectiveness of unison

production overall for this population and that metrical timing may confer an even stronger benefit

to accuracy.

Fluent PWAs did not show this relationship between accuracy and timing, as only two of

the eight participants had a significant timing advantage in the metrical condition, one of whom

achieved a substantially higher metrical accuracy score. There are a number of possible

explanations, though we recognize that they are somewhat speculative. First, as we have

suggested earlier, perhaps fluent PWAs do not need to rely as heavily on metrical structure as an

external scaffold to make predictions about upcoming targets and/or to generate timing

frameworks for their productions, as they are more able to rely on their relatively spared lexical

and syntactic processing resources to do so. Thus, their performance may in fact be similar across

generally comparable performance in metrical and conversational conditions, with a small benefit

Conclusions

Overall, our preliminary findings support the idea that PWAs entrain during unison

production and that speaking along with metrically regular prosodic patterns facilitates temporal

prediction thereby supporting subsequent planning and production. This effect was most

pronounced in nonfluent PWAs in terms of both accuracy and timing of spoken output, which is

consistent with the longstanding clinical intuition that nonfluent PWAs are ideal candidates for

treatment approaches that employ unison production and/or metrical rhythm. However, benefits

associated with metrical stimuli were also observed for some fluent PWAs in this study, as well

as for control participants. These findings overall add to the evidence that rhythmic regularity may

generally aid spoken language processing across a variety of individuals—not just those with

restricted spoken output.

Limitations

There are some limitations of this study that are important to keep in mind. With regard to

our procedure, the present study employed a listen-then-repeat paradigm, which means that

participants became familiar with the stimuli before repeating them. In addition to facilitating

temporal predictability—the focus of this study—familiarity can also enhance lexical and semantic

prediction. To address this, we made an effort to match our metrical and conversational stimuli

such that prosodic timing structure was the only meaningful difference. However, we cannot

entirely rule out potential effects due to differences in lexical/semantic predictability between the

sentence stimuli for different timing conditions. In addition, the sample size is relatively small,

especially for subgroups of PWAs. Generalizability may also be limited by the lack of

representational diversity within our sample, which we plan to address in future recruitment

endeavors. In addition, while we broadly dichotomized PWAs here based on fluency, we

recognize that it does not adequately reflect the multidimensional nature of fluency (Gordon &

Clough, 2022), nor can it account for the substantial within-group heterogeneity in our sample.

differences in performance, the present study did not specifically address the potential

relationships among specific cognitive, linguistic, and motor abilities that may be associated with

more success in metrical timing conditions. Some limitations in our statistical approach should

also be noted, particularly with regard to the timing alignment data for PWAs: We utilized Mann–

## Introduction

The study described in Chapter 2 investigated the effect of prosodic timing structure on

(1) overall accuracy of sentences produced in unison with a spoken model, and (2) overall timing

alignment between the participant speech and the unison model. Group-level comparisons

revealed a greater percentage of accurate syllables produced under metrical timing compared to

conversational timing, and that metrically timed speech was produced both earlier (i.e., with

greater anticipation/less lag) between the participant’s output and the unison model), and with

less variability in time (lower standard deviations) relative to a unison model. We interpreted these

findings as evidence that the regularity of the metrical timing condition facilitated temporal

prediction, enabling better entrainment—a process described to support spoken production in

people with aphasia (Fridriksson et al., 2012; Quique et al., 2022).

The present chapter builds upon the previous study in several ways. The primary addition

is an investigation of the role of phrasal stress in our stimuli, to determine whether phrasally

stressed syllables differ from unstressed syllables in production accuracy and unison timing

alignment. The introduction that follows will describe the motivation for this exploration, including

the significance of phrasally stressed syllables as a feature of both conversationally timed and

metrically timed stimuli. A second addition is in the statistical approach. While the prior study

analyzed differences in central tendency across conditions, the present study implements

syllable-level regression models to directly examine which features of our experimental conditions

(unison vs. solo production) and stimuli (metrical vs. conversational timing, phrasally stressed vs.

unstressed syllables) predict production accuracy and facilitate temporal prediction. Finally, the

present chapter expands the data set, including additional people with aphasia (PWAs) and

control participants.

Defining phrasal stress

Chapter 2 introduced the contrast between metrically timed versus conversationally timed

sentences, arising from differences in the patterning of prominent, phrasally “stressed” syllables

versus non-prominent, “unstressed” syllables in each sentence type. While the patterns differ

across these two types of timing structures, both sentence types contain some syllables that are

stressed and some that are unstressed. There are important differences between stressed and

unstressed syllables—in terms of acoustic and linguistic properties, and in terms of how they are

perceived and produced—that make it logical to ask whether the beneficial effects of unison

production and/or metrical timing observed in Chapter 2 apply to all syllables, or specifically to

stressed syllables. Before discussing these differences and their implications in detail, we must

clearly define stress as it applies to the present study.

Stress has been described as “the linguistic manifestation of rhythmic structure” (Hayes,

1995, p. 1). It is a prosodic feature of many languages, characterized by the marking of a word or

syllable in a way that increases its salience relative to the surrounding context, sometimes termed

“phonetic enhancement” (Franich, 2022).  In spoken languages, stressed syllables are often

acoustically-phonetically enhanced compared to unstressed syllables, marked by longer duration,

greater intensity, and more extreme fundamental frequency  (Cole et al., 2019; Lehiste, 1970; see

also introduction to Franich, 2022).

In terms of English linguistic structure, there are two types of stress that are defined in

nested, hierarchical levels (Beckman & Edwards, 1994). Lexical stress refers to stress at the

single-word level, and can be most clearly illustrated in the context of multisyllabic words, where

one syllable is “stronger” than the others (e.g., baNAna, where capital letters indicate the stressed

syllable). Moving up the hierarchy, phrasal stress (also called sentence stress) refers to the

emphasis placed on one or more words within a phrase that signal(s) new and/or important

information to the listener. One way this can be illustrated is via sentences that contain the same


<!-- Page 79 -->


61

words, but contrast in the location of phrasal stress.1 In the sentence “She bought him a YEllow

banana”, the placement of phrasal stress (bold text) on the word “yellow” indicates the speaker’s

intent to clarify the color of the banana. In contrast, in the sentence, “She bought him a yellow

baNAna”, the speaker clarifies which type of yellow item was bought. Typically, the lexically

stressed syllable (shown in capital letters) within a phrasally stressed word is marked with a pitch

excursion, known as a pitch accent (Bolinger, 1958). Thus, a syllable can bear both lexical stress

as feature of the word structure, and phrasal stress as a feature of the phrase prosody. The

present study focuses on the role of phrasally stressed syllables, as they create the contrastive

patterns between our metrical and conversational sentence stimuli. However, the following

sections will review relevant literature pertaining to stress at both levels, as the rationale, design,

and findings of many of these studies overlap substantially and are therefore useful to consider

collectively.

Stressed syllables in spoken language perception and production

A number of studies involving individuals with typical speech/language abilities have

revealed processing advantages for phrasally stressed versus unstressed syllables, often by

investigating how rapidly and/or accurately participants detect specified targets embedded within

each type of syllable. For example, multiple studies have revealed that embedding targets within

stressed syllables leads to faster reaction times for target phonemes (Cutler, 1976; Cutler & Foss,

1977; Fiveash et al., 2021; Pitt & Samuel, 1990; Shields et al., 1974), and better accuracy in

detecting mispronunciations (R. A. Cole & Jakimik, 1980), vowel perturbations (Zheng &

Pierrehumbert, 2010), and word changes (Falk & Dalla Bella, 2016), and in recalling previously

heard target syllables (Gow & Gordon, 1993). In addition, tongue twister production experiments

have shown that phrasally stressed syllables are produced with fewer errors compared to

A smaller set of studies has investigated relationships among syllable stress and spoken

Multiple experiments have shown that PWAs respond more accurately to comprehension

questions after listening to passages where target words were emphasized with phrasal stress,

compared to control conditions where there was no emphatic phrasal stress on target words

(Kimelman, 1999; Kimelman & McNeil, 1987). Similarly, emphatic phrasal stress has been shown

to improve reaction time and accuracy of semantic judgements in PWAs (Slansky & McNeil,

1997). With regard to production accuracy, most investigations have focused on the role of lexical

are more prone to errors, particularly in word-initial position (Aichert et al., 2016, 2019; Howard &

Smith, 2002; Nickels & Howard, 1999; though see Odell et al., 1991 for conflicting results). Similar

patterns have been revealed at the phrase level: Goodglass et al. (1967) found PWAs produced

phrase-initial unstressed functor words with more errors (or omitted them entirely), than when the

same words were produced with phrasal stress. One report of sentence repetition found that

people with AOS produced fewer errors on phrasally stressed content words (Tonkovich &

Marquardt, 1977). Finally, in one of the tongue twister studies described above, Kember et al.

(2017) found the same benefit of phrasal stress for people with dysarthria.

Overall, it appears that stressed syllables are advantaged in perception and production in

people with and without acquired communication disorders. However, as several studies with

PWAs note, relationships among stress and accuracy are complex and may depend on factors

related to linguistic structure as well as clinical characteristics of the participants (Goodglass et

al., 1967; Howard & Smith, 2002; see also Biran & Friedmann, 2005). As such, one aim of the

present study is to determine whether phrasally stressed syllables are produced more accurately

than unstressed syllables in our prosodically controlled sentence repetition task, which was
