designed to systematically examine factors (unison production and metrical timing) that promote

accuracy of spoken output in people with aphasia.

Conditions that enhance temporal predictability

Why might stressed syllables be advantaged in perception and production? Some studies

have proposed that the increased salience of phrasally stressed syllables may aid listeners in

allocating attentional resources toward those syllables (Cutler, 1976; Pitt & Samuel, 1990; Shields

et al., 1974). Testing this attentional allocation idea, Cutler (1976) spliced acoustically identical

target words into sentences with differing intonational contours and found that participants were

faster at detecting phonemes within target words that were predicted to be stressed based on the

surrounding context. She interpreted this as evidence that predicting the location of upcoming

stressed syllables is “an integral part of sentence understanding” (p. 58). This idea later evolved

into the attentional bounce hypothesis, empirically tested by Pitt and Samuel (1990) through a

series of experiments using two-syllable words. In typical sentence contexts (akin to the

conversationally timed stimuli in Chapter 2), participants were more accurate, but not faster, at

detecting target phonemes in syllables predicted to be stressed versus unstressed (Experiment

1). In a follow up experiment, they used lists of two-syllable words, in which all words had stress

on either the first or second syllable, creating regularly alternating patterns of stressed and

unstressed syllables (akin in prosodic structure to our metrical stimuli). Here, they found that

participants were faster and more accurate at detecting phonemes in syllables predicted to be

stressed versus unstressed (Experiment 2), and that this finding did not generalize to word lists

with unpredictable lexical stress patterns (Experiment 3). They therefore suggest that anticipating

the location of stressed syllables does play a role in typical spoken language processing but is

enhanced substantially in contexts that are more rhythmically predictable.

Accordingly, an increasing body of research has examined how rhythmic regularity

(henceforth “metrical timing,” as in Chapter 2) may influence spoken language processing. Target


<!-- Page 82 -->


64

phonemes in stressed syllables were shown to be detected faster when syllables aligned with the

timing of strong beats predicted from the preceding metrical stimulus (Cason et al., 2015; Cason

& Schön, 2012; Quené & Port, 2005). In a more nuanced examination of metrical timing structure

and spoken language processing, Fiveash et al. (2021) conducted a syllable monitoring task using

metrically timed sentences in which participants were primed with metronome cues presented

either at the rate of phrasally stressed syllables, or at the rate of all syllables. Participants who

heard the phrasal stress prime earlier in the experiment were faster at detecting phrasally

stressed syllables versus unstressed syllables and were faster at this task than participants who

heard syllable-level primes first. There was no difference in reaction times to stressed versus

unstressed syllables for participants who heard syllable-level primes first. Thus, metrical stimuli

can establish top-down temporal expectations of phrasal stress structure and enhance processing

of phrasally stressed syllables. (See introduction to Chapter 2, as well as Beier & Ferreira, 2018

for additional examples of metrical timing and spoken language processing.) Building on this idea,

an additional aim of the present study is to determine whether the temporal predictability of

phrasally stressed syllables yields earlier timing during production when speaking along with a

unison model, and whether metrical timing enhances this effect.

Which aspects of temporal predictability benefit spoken output in PWAs?

Overall, the literature reviewed in the introduction so far suggests that (1) stressed

syllables (both at lexical and phrasal levels) are advantaged in speech/language processing and

production, possibly due to increased attentional resource allocation, and (2) metrical timing,

which enhances temporal predictability, can affect the processing of stressed syllables. From a

clinical perspective, these points are of particular interest in considering possible mechanisms of

unison production approaches for aphasia and AOS (reviewed more extensively in Chapter 2),

as stressed syllables are often the “locus of coordination” in speech synchronization behaviors

(Franich, 2022, p. 2, and references therein). Furthermore, a subset of unison treatment


<!-- Page 83 -->


65

approaches for aphasia use musical/beat-based prosodic timing, which typically involves

differentiating phrasally stressed syllables from unstressed syllables via higher pitch and/or

increased duration (Hurkmans et al., 2015; Norton et al., 2009; Van Eeckhout, 2010).  In addition,

multiple studies have revealed that metrical timing can increase overall accuracy of spoken

sentence production in PWAs/people with AOS  (e.g., Dworkin et al., 1988; Kershenbaum et al.,

2023; Racette et al., 2006; Stahl et al., 2011). However, the extent to which unison production

and/or metrical timing might differentially affect the production of stressed versus unstressed

syllables remains unclear.

Combining insights about phrasal stress, metrical timing, and unison production, a recent

study by Quique et al. (2022) found that PWAs were able to produce scripted sentences more

accurately following unison production treatment in which external rhythmic cues were added to

the model recordings, either aligned with the stressed syllables, or occurring with metrical

regularity throughout the sentence. Both types of rhythmic cues provided equivalent benefit to

overall production accuracy, but specific analysis of whether stressed versus unstressed syllables

were produced more accurately was not undertaken in that study. Thus, while a growing body of

work suggests that phrasal stress, unison production, and metrical timing can each benefit spoken

output in PWAs, it is unclear whether the increased temporal predictability of metrical contexts

and/or the scaffolding provided by unison production benefit the “beat-bearing” stressed syllables

specifically, or all syllables more generally.

As such, a third aim of the present work is to explore possible relationships among

accuracy, temporal predictability, and phrasal stress among PWAs. Understanding these

relationships can provide further insight into the mechanism by which unison production benefits

PWAs. We have previously proposed that unison production works by way of entrainment—a

process of predicting the timing of upcoming events in an external stimulus in order to produce

actions in time with that stimulus. The act of speaking in unison with a model requires the PWA

to generate temporal predictions about upcoming syllables, which may facilitate planning and


<!-- Page 84 -->


66

production of spoken output. Factors that enhance predictability may therefore further benefit

production. Results reported in Chapter 2 supported this idea, revealing through separate

analyses of temporal prediction and production accuracy that metrical timing benefits each during

unison production. Studies reviewed in this introduction suggest that stressed syllables are also

advantaged in temporal prediction (determined via perception studies) and production accuracy

(revealed in solo repetition). However, we have not directly explored the relationship between

temporal predictability and syllable production accuracy during unison production based on

metrical timing or stress status. If syllables that are better temporally predicted (produced earlier

in time) are also produced more accurately, this would provide more direct evidence for

entrainment as an underlying mechanism of unison production. Investigating stressed versus

unstressed syllables separately can shed more light on the nature of this mechanism: If the

advantaged status of phrasally stressed syllables is further enhanced during unison production

and/or metrical timing, this may suggest that the benefit associated with these facilitating contexts

is driven by amplifying resource allocation to those syllables specifically. However, it may be the

case that unison production and/or metrical timing aid prediction and production all syllables

equally. In either case, understanding how these variables relate to each other can provide

specific insight into how unison production works, which may have implications for designing

stimulus sentences that maximize treatment gains.

The present study

The present study is an exploratory investigation of the role of phrasal stress during PWAs’

sentence production under multiple speaking conditions, leveraging data collected for the study

reported in Chapter 2. In that study, we found that PWAs repeat sentences more accurately when

speaking in unison with a model (compared to repeating solo), and both PWAs and controls

produce unison sentences more accurately when sentences are metrically timed. In addition, we

found that metrical timing enhanced temporal prediction for both groups, as quantified by the


<!-- Page 85 -->


67

earlier and even anticipatory timing alignment of participant productions relative to the unison

model. Given the evidence that phrasally stressed (henceforth “stressed”) syllables may be

advantaged in perception and production, possibly due to enhanced temporal predictability (Beier

& Ferreira, 2018; Pitt & Samuel, 1990), and that the main contrast between our metrical and

conversational sentence stimuli is the patterning of stressed versus unstressed syllables, it is

important to understand how these variables may intersect. We investigate these ideas

systematically via the following exploratory Aims, and discuss potential hypotheses for each Aim

below.

Aim 1 focuses on production accuracy during sentence repetition, in which we ask whether

PWAs and/or controls repeat stressed syllables more accurately than unstressed syllables.

Additionally, we explore whether the effect differs based on production condition (unison vs. solo)

and/or prosodic timing condition (metrical vs. conversational sentence timing). We hypothesize

no effect of syllable stress among control participants. For PWAs, we hypothesize that overall,

stressed syllables will be produced more accurately than unstressed syllables across production

and timing conditions, and that the effect may be enhanced under metrical timing (and possibly

unison production), as the stressed syllables are made even more salient and predictable in the

context of a metrical structure. However, an alternative possibility is that metrical timing and/or

unison production improve production accuracy of all syllables, such that any beneficial effects of

phrasal stress are limited to the less predictable/scaffolded conditions of solo production and/or

conversational timing.

Aim 2 focuses on temporal predictability, as measured by comparing the timing alignment

between participant productions and stimuli in the unison condition. We ask whether PWAs and/or

controls produce stressed syllables with earlier timing alignment compared to unstressed

syllables, and whether the effect differs based whether sentences are metrically timed versus

conversationally timed. For both groups, we hypothesize that stressed syllables will be more

temporally predictable overall, such that timing alignment of stressed syllables will be earlier than


<!-- Page 86 -->


68

of unstressed syllables. We additionally hypothesize that this effect will be more pronounced for

metrically timed sentences, as we previously found that metrical timing leads to earlier-timed

productions overall (see Chapter 2). However, like our accuracy hypothesis, an alternative

possibility is that metrical timing enhances predictability of both stressed and unstressed syllables,

to the extent that any differential benefit of phrasal stress will be limited to conversationally timed

sentences, where temporal predictability is lower overall.

Finally, Aim 3 is the most exploratory, in which we examine relationships among accuracy,

timing alignment and phrasal stress to gain insight into the mechanism of unison production. We

hypothesize that syllables that are better temporally predicted (i.e., produced earlier in time

relative to the unison model) are more likely to be produced accurately, and further examine

whether this relationship differs for metrically timed versus conversationally timed sentences,

and/or for phrasally stressed versus unstressed syllables.

Stimuli and Experimental Procedure

Stimuli and experimental procedure were identical to those described in the Method

section of Chapter 2. They are summarized here for clarity, but readers should refer to Chapter 2

for specific details. Briefly, stimuli consisted of 12 sentences with a metrical prosodic structure

and 12 with a conversational prosodic structure, audio recorded by a female speaker in a

soundproof booth. Metrically timed sentences contained repeating patterns of phrasally stressed

(S) versus unstressed (u) syllables (e.g., S-u-S-u, or S-u-u-S-u-u), while conversationally timed

sentences did not have repeating patterns. (See Figure 2.2A in Chapter 2 for a graphical

representation.) Sentences were developed in pairs to maximize lexical and phonological

similarity, while contrasting in prosodic timing structure (e.g.,“ASK me for EGGS at the MARket”

[metrical] vs. “reTURN the EGGS at the MARket” [conversational].) Metrically timed sentences

were recorded at a syllable rate of 2 Hz (120 beats per minute). Conversational sentences were

recorded using natural prosody and matched in duration to each metrical counterpart sentence.

Metrical were preceded by a lead-in sequence of metronome clicks generated based on the

metrical pattern of the sentence, while conversational sentences were always preceded by 4

metronome clicks.

During the experiment, participants listened to the sentences through over-the-ear

headphones, and then repeated them in two production conditions. During “solo” trials,

participants were instructed to listen to each sentence twice, and then repeat the sentence by

themselves. During “unison” trials, the sentence was presented three times: The participant

listened to the sentence twice, and then produced it in unison with the recording on the third

repetition. Thus, the 2 x 2 design (PRODUCTION CONDITION x TIMING CONDITION) yielded four

contrasts: Metrical Solo, Conversational Solo, Metrical Unison, and Conversational Unison.

Sentences were presented in pseudorandomized blocks by production condition to minimize the

cognitive load of alternating task demands. Audacity software (Audacity Team, 2021) was used


<!-- Page 91 -->


73

to present all stimulus sentences and record all participant productions. Unison trials were time

locked to the stimuli so that timing alignment between participant productions and the unison

stimuli could be evaluated. Line delay (presentation-to-recording delay) was documented at the

start of each experimental session for adjustment during analysis.

Stimulus rating: Determining phrasally stressed versus unstressed syllables

While stimuli were designed such that metrical sentences had obvious, regular patterns

of phrasal syllable stress and conversational sentences did not, the goals of the present study

required us to determine specifically which syllables in the conversational stimuli bear phrasal

stress. Past studies of phrasal stress perception in conversationally timed sentence contexts have

shown that listeners can vary substantially in which words they rate as “prominent” (Kakouros &

Räsänen, 2016; Mo et al., 2008; You, 2012). Therefore, rather than basing phrasal stress

assignment on the judgements of the first author, we opted for a systematic approach by

averaging ratings collected from multiple naïve listeners.

Five research assistants (RAs) with minimal to no familiarity with the stimuli in the present

study independently labeled the phrasal stress of the sentences after meeting with the first author

over videoconference for an orientation to the task. Each RA was provided a Microsoft Powerpoint

slide deck containing task instructions and two practice sentences, followed by a series of

individual slides for each of the 24 (12 metrical + 12 conversational) study stimuli. Though our

main motivation was to obtain phrasal stress ratings for syllables in conversational sentences,

metrical sentences were included for comparison to verify comprehension of the task. To avoid

potential order effects, sentence order was randomized in each presentation order, with the

exception that counterpart sentences (i.e., a corresponding pair of metrical and conversational

sentences) had to be separated by at least two intervening sentences.  Each stimulus slide had

one written sentence in the middle of the slide, and an audio icon in the lower left corner that

would play the corresponding sound file when clicked. To facilitate labeling, individual syllables


<!-- Page 92 -->


74

within multisyllabic words were separated by periods. Syllabification adhered to the Maximum

Onset Principle (Kahn, 1976) and was further verified with a syllabified version of CMU

Pronouncing Dictionary (1998; Bartlett et al., 2009). RAs were instructed to listen to each

sentence, and mark syllables that sounded “emphasized” or “prominent” in bold red text. Syllables

that RAs thought might be emphasized, or sound “partially emphasized” were to be marked with

italic text. RAs could listen to each sentence as many times as they wished, but were encouraged

to “go with their gut” perception regarding prominence.

RA ratings were converted to a trichotomous scoring system, with 0 for unmarked (non-

prominent) syllables, 0.5 for possibly or partially prominent syllables, and 1 for prominent

syllables. Ratings for each syllable were then averaged across all RAs, and any syllable with an

average score ≥ 0.75 was considered phrasally stressed in subsequent analyses. All others were

considered phrasally unstressed. Figure 3.1 shows the distribution of average rating scores in

each condition.

Data scoring: Unison timing alignment

The process for determining unison timing alignment between participant productions and

stimulus sentences was exactly as described in Chapter 2. In summary, we compared the voice


<!-- Page 95 -->


77

onset moment (VOM; the timing at which voicing begins) of obstruent-initial target syllables in

participant productions and stimuli. VOM was chosen as the point of comparison as (1) it is an

acoustic landmark that is relatively efficient to detect in the audio signal, and (2) it roughly

corresponds to the syllable’s “p-center,” a timepoint hypothesized as the location of the “beat” of

a syllable, and the point at which people have been shown to synchronize (Franich, 2022; Morton

et al., 1976). These VOM timepoints were used to calculate timing offset values for each target

syllable, defined as the signed difference in time between the participant’s VOM and the

corresponding VOM in the recorded stimulus sentence, subtracting line delay. Positive offsets

indicate that the participant’s production lagged the stimulus recording, while negative offsets

indicate that the participant spoke ahead of the stimulus, which we suggest is evidence of

temporal prediction. Importantly, target syllables were phonemically identical across each

metrical-conversational sentence pair to maximize comparability across prosodic timing

conditions (see Table A.1 for a complete list of stimuli).

VOMs were extracted from target syllables via a semi-automated procedure, using the

autoVOT plugin for Praat speech analysis software (Boersma & Weenink, 2021; Keshet et al.,

2014). We used Praat textgrids to manually isolate time windows around each target syllable

onset, which included the release burst of the initial obstruent consonant, four consecutive cycles

of voicing, and approximately 30 ms of padding on either side (see Chapter 2, Figure 2.3). These

time windows and associated audio files were input to the autoVOT plugin for Praat, which uses

a trained classifier to automatically detect and label multiple acoustic landmarks of voice onset

time within the specified time window (though the present study focused only on the VOM

landmark). During the window isolation process, any syllable productions that contained

phonemic errors, phonetic distortions, irregular pitch periods (“creaky voice”), or other possible

ambiguities were flagged for review. After running autoVOT, VOM timepoints were adjusted

manually as needed.

A maximum of 64 timing offset values (32 metrical + 32 conversational targets) were

computed for each participant, including for syllables produced with errors, as the present study

analyzes timing alignment separately from production accuracy. We made every effort to extract

VOM from all target syllables, however some participants had fewer than 64 total time points due

to (1) complete omission of the syllable, (2) no voicing of a vowel (e.g., “k—” for “con”), (3)

syllables for which the obstruent onset timing was too ambiguous to manually determine a search

window, and (4) audio recording error during data collection. Together, this resulted in

missing/excluded data for 11% of possible target syllables across PWAs (ranging from 1 to 19

missing targets per PWA), and for < 2% for possible targets across controls (ranging from 1 to 25

As a final preprocessing step, we excluded timing offset values that fell outside of +/- 2.5

All statistical analyses were conducted in R, version 4.3.1 (R Core Team, 2023). Unless

otherwise noted below, all models were fit using the lme4 package, version 1.1-35.1 (Bates et al.,

2015), and p-values were computed using the lmerTest package, version 3.1-3 (Kuznetsova et

al., 2017). For logistic regression models, the lme4 optimizer was set to ‘bobyqa’ to avoid model

were investigated using the emmeans package, version 1.10.0 (Lenth, 2024). For readability,

model statistics for relevant results are reported in the Results section. However, full model

outputs for each analysis are included in the Appendix (Table A.3 through Table A.7).

To investigate the effects of phrasal stress, metrical timing, and unison production on

accuracy of syllable production (Aim 1), we fit separate mixed-effects logistic regression models

for controls and PWAs. These models included a crossed fixed-effects structure for experimental

predictors (PRODUCTION CONDITION * TIMING CONDITION * PHRASAL STRESS), and random intercepts

for participants. Reference categories for the predictors in this model were SOLO,

CONVERSATIONAL, and UNSTRESSED, respectively. AOS CONSTRUCT SCORE was included as a

covariate in the PWA model, and AGE (in years) was included as a covariate in the control model.

Age was not included as a covariate for PWAs as it was confounded by the heterogeneity of

clinical presentations across ages in our sample.

In both models, syllable accuracy was considered as a strict binary variable, where

syllables with any errors were considered incorrect. However, we note that such a strict approach

to accuracy could potentially obscure more nuanced relationships among production accuracy

and our experimental predictors, particularly for PWAs. Indeed, a notable percentage of syllable

productions among PWAs included syllables with only one phonemic error (e.g., “gog” for “dog”,

see Figure 3.6). Clinically, such productions can often be intelligible in context (Nicholas &

Brookshire, 1993), and could be considered a meaningful “intermediate” category of correctness

that might be separately predicted by one or more of our predictors. Thus, using the same fixed-

and random-effects model structure, we fit a mixed-effects multinomial logistic regression model

using the mclogit package, version 0.9.6 (Elff, 2024). In this model, the outcome contained three

categories of correctness: incorrect, one phonemic error, and correct. A multinomial model was

chosen rather than an ordinal model despite the ordered nature of the accuracy categories, as


<!-- Page 100 -->


82

our data did not meet the proportional odds assumption required for this model, determined

graphically using the procedure in Harrell (2015; p. 316).

To determine the effects of phrasal stress and metrical timing on unison timing alignment

(our measure of temporal predictability; Aim 2), we ran separate mixed-effects linear models for

controls and PWAs, with signed timing offset for each target syllable as the outcome. Signed

timing offset was used rather than absolute timing offset, as our hypotheses concerned prediction

(indicated by earlier-occurring productions) rather than absolute synchrony. The fixed- and

random-effects structure for each of these models was the same as for the accuracy models,

except that PRODUCTION CONDITION was not included since timing offset data existed only for

productions in the unison condition.

To explore possible relationships among accuracy, unison timing alignment, and phrasal

stress among PWAs (Aim 3), we visually inspected graphs of the timing offset data, stratified by

accuracy, across the levels TIMING CONDITION and PHRASAL STRESS. The relationship could not be

formally modeled with logistic regression, due to the difference in ranges of timing offset values

for the two prosodic timing conditions, which would lead to model overfitting and uninterpretable

odds ratios.

## Results

## Discussion

This study was an exploratory, secondary analysis of the effect of phrasal stress on

spoken output in PWAs and controls with typical speech and language abilities. The experimental

task was a sentence repetition task in a 2 x 2 design in which participants produced metrically  or

conversationally timed sentences (TIMING CONDITION) in solo repetition or in unison with an audio

recorded model (PRODUCTION CONDITION). This enabled us to examine possible main effects of

stress, as well as potential interactions between stress and speaking conditions demonstrated to

support spoken output among PWAs (unison production and metrical timing). Aim 1 focused on

whether one or more of these factors improved accuracy of syllable production, while Aim 2

focused on whether they improved temporal prediction, as measured by participant-stimulus


<!-- Page 115 -->


97

timing alignment during unison production. Finally, Aim 3 was an informal exploration of the

relationship between accuracy and temporal prediction, stratified by these factors of interest. The

following discussion will describe key findings and interpretations for each Aim.

Aim 1: Syllable production accuracy

Control participants made very few errors, which was expected, as the sentences were

not designed to be taxing for typical speakers. As such, there was no effect of phrasal stress on

production accuracy, nor any interactions with production condition or timing condition. Unison

production hindered accuracy overall—a finding not observed in the sentence-level analyses of

Chapter 2, but consistent with observations that unison speech is more effortful and less natural

for speakers without speech/language difficulties (Ingham et al., 2009). An additional finding,

made possible by the inclusion of a cohort of younger controls, was that likelihood of error

production increased very slightly with age.

Interestingly, controls appeared to exhibit a strong metrical benefit, in that of the few errors

produced overall (159 out of 18,851 total syllables), the vast majority (120) were in

conversationally timed sentences. However, it is worth noting that within those conversational

errors, over half were attributable to errors on four syllables across sentences. While we cannot

rule out the possibility that these specific stimuli were surprising or challenging in some way we

did not expect, we did not observe this same disproportionate rate of errors on those syllables

among PWAs. Furthermore, the identical counterpart syllables within the metrical condition were

produced at a far lower error rate. Overall, this may suggest that metrical timing aids speakers in

attending to and/or coordinating production of syllables that may be more vulnerable in

conversationally timed sentences, and this effect was only revealed for a small proportion of our

relatively simple sentences. Future research could examine possible differential effects of

prosodic timing structure in sentences designed to induce a greater error rate among typical

speakers, such as tongue twisters (as in Croot et al., 2010; Kember et al., 2017).


<!-- Page 116 -->


98

Production accuracy among PWAs was investigated via two separate models. The first

model was based on the same stringent accuracy criteria used for controls, in that syllables were

binarily scored as correct versus incorrect, wherein any syllable with at least one phonemic error

(including omission) was scored as incorrect. In this stringent model, there was no main effect of

phrasal stress, nor any interactions between phrasal stress and production condition or timing

condition. There were also no main effects of production condition (though it trended toward

unison benefit) or timing condition, but a significant interaction between the two indicates that the

combination of unison production and metrical timing gives rise to more accurate syllable

production. This aligns with past findings by Racette et al. (2006), who found a benefit of metrical

timing (via singing) for PWAs only in unison production, not in solo repetition. In summary, this

view of the data suggests that while speaking along with metrically timed sentences promotes

syllable production accuracy among PWAs, the effects are not driven by improvement in the

“beat-bearing” stressed syllables specifically. Rather, it is likely that accuracy of all syllables

improves.

Our second model was a multinomial logistic regression based on a trichotomous

approach to accuracy scoring, in that syllables scored as “incorrect” in the first model were now

subdivided into categories of “partially correct” syllables with only one phonemic error (1PhE),

versus fully incorrect syllables that contained more than one phonemic error (or were fully

omitted). This more lenient view of accuracy acknowledges that productions with slight errors can

often be considered intelligible in context, and that they might also represent clinically meaningful

benefit from facilitatory speaking conditions, even if the output is not strictly accurate. The results

of this model present a similar picture to the stricter model, with some key differences. First, a

main effect of phrasal stress was revealed, such that the odds of a syllable being produced at

least partially accurately were higher for stressed syllables. This finding was significant for 1PhE

syllables, and very close to significant (p = 0.051) for fully correct syllables. Additionally, this model

contrasts with the previous “strict” model in that, when scoring trichotomously, unison production


<!-- Page 117 -->


99

predicts at least partially accurate production, with a far stronger effect for 1PhE syllables than

correct syllables. This suggests that speaking in unison with a model can aid PWAs in producing

syllables that may be more accurate, even if not fully accurate. It is important to note that the

“incorrect” category in our scoring framework does not differentiate between syllables produced

with errors and syllables that were completely omitted. Syllable omission was not uncommon for

participants with severe aphasia, who in some cases, did not produce entire words or phrases

within stimuli, particularly in the solo condition. With that caveat in mind, another related

interpretation is that unison production aids PWAs in attempting syllables that they might not

otherwise produce in solo contexts. Finally, as in the stricter model, there was a significant

interaction between production condition and timing condition for correct syllables, which

suggests speaking in unison with metrically timed sentences helps PWAs be more precisely

accurate.

Synthesizing insights across accuracy models, a few ideas emerge: First, during sentence

repetition, phrasal stress may increase the likelihood that PWAs will produce syllables more

accurately, but this effect is only observable with a nuanced scoring approach that accounts for

intermediate levels of accuracy, rather than a binary correct/incorrect classification system. While

this secondary analysis is not fully comparable to prior work on stress and production accuracy in

PWAs, mostly due to differences in stimulus design, one commonality in the findings is that the

relationship between stress and accuracy is multifaceted, and cannot be captured through basic

dichotomous classification of stress and/or accuracy (e.g., Aichert et al., 2016; Goodglass et al.,

1967; Howard & Smith, 2002). Second, the effects of both unison production and metrical timing

may be considered additive, in that unison production alone may help PWAs produce more

syllables overall, including those that are at least partially accurate, but speaking along with

metrically timed sentences yields productions that are more precisely accurate (see Figure 3.7).

This supports our proposal that unison production works by way of entrainment: The unison model

provides a prosodic timing scaffold that facilitates planning and production of spoken output, and


<!-- Page 118 -->


100

when that model has a rhythmically regular prosodic structure, the scaffold is more stable and

predictable, freeing up additional cognitive resources that contribute to more accurate production.

Aim 2: Temporal prediction

We investigated temporal prediction by comparing the timing alignment of target syllables

in participants’ spoken output and the audio-recorded stimuli during unison speech production.

Target syllables were identical across metrical and conversational sentence pairs. First, we

confirm that, just as in Chapter 2, there was a main effect of timing condition for both PWAs and

controls, such that syllables produced in metrically timed sentences were produced earlier in time

than their conversationally timed counterparts. Furthermore, comparing the model coefficients,

the effect was stronger for PWAs than for controls, which suggests that metrical timing is

especially beneficial for individuals who may have more difficulty using linguistic knowledge to

extract temporal information from typical sentence contexts. Again, controls’ productions were

generally synchronous with both types of sentences, whereas PWAs tended to lag slightly (see

*Figure 3.9 and Figure 3.11).*

The primary aim of the present investigation was to compare temporal prediction of

stressed versus unstressed syllables. We hypothesized that stressed syllables in our stimuli

would be more temporally predictable overall (e.g., Cutler, 1976; Pitt & Samuel, 1990), and this

would be evident in that they would be produced earlier in time (i.e., with lower timing offset

values) in unison production. The two-way interaction between PHRASAL STRESS and TIMING

CONDITION revealed that this hypothesis was partially correct: In conversationally timed

sentences, both PWAs and controls produced stressed syllables earlier in time than unstressed

syllables. This aligns with ideas put forth by Shields et al. (1974), and Cutler (1976), later

formalized by Pitt and Samuel (1990) as the attentional bounce hypothesis, which suggests that

listeners make use information in the speech signal to predict the locations of stressed syllables.

Evidence for this hypothesis was based on perception tasks (i.e., phoneme monitoring), and the


<!-- Page 119 -->


101

present finding in our conversational stimuli lends further support via a unison speech production

task, which required participants to extract temporal information in order to predict and

subsequently synchronize spoken output with upcoming targets.

A more surprising result was that in metrically timed sentences, we found the opposite

relationship between timing alignment and phrasal stress, such that unstressed syllables were

produced earlier in time than stressed syllables. This was contrary to our hypothesis that,

particularly within a rhythmically regular prosodic structure, the “beat-bearing” syllables would be

easier to temporally predict, and therefore be produced with less delay (or even anticipatorily—

see Chapter 2). While this finding is puzzling, it parallels results reported in a rhythmic finger

tapping study conducted by Slis et al. (2023). Adults who stutter and typical controls were asked

to tap along with click sequences that varied in rhythmic complexity. When tapping along to a

repeating strong-weak-weak-weak beat sequence, both groups of participants tapped more

synchronously and more forcefully on strong beats, while tapping ahead of the weak beats and

with less force. The authors suggest this pattern of results can be explained by the sensory

accumulator model (SAM; Aschersleben, 2002). For context, the SAM was developed to explain

the somewhat mysterious phenomenon of the “negative mean asynchrony” commonly observed

in sensorimotor synchronization research, in which participants who are attempting to tap in time

with metrically regular stimuli (such as metronome clicks) tend to slightly anticipate the beat (e.g.,

Repp & Su, 2013). The SAM proposes that for auditory (metronome) and tactile (finger tap)

sensations to be perceived as occurring synchronously, a central representation must be

generated that combines input from both sensory systems. This central representation forms once

enough sensory information accumulates in each modality to reach an activation threshold.

However, the systems are not equal in how quickly and how much information must accumulate

before that threshold is reached—and the model assumes that auditory information accumulates

faster than tactile information. Thus, for both sensations to reach the activation threshold at the

same time, leading to the perception of synchrony, the tactile sensation must begin the


<!-- Page 120 -->


102

accumulation process earlier, meaning taps must occur earlier in time than the auditory beat. The

SAM also assumes that more intense sensation—for example, a more forceful finger tap—can

accelerate sensory accumulation. Forceful taps will consequently not require as much lead time

as weaker taps to elicit an equivalent central perception of finger tap-auditory beat synchrony.

These predictions of the SAM were therefore borne out by the differences in observed tap timing

and force for strong and weak beats in Slis et al. (2023).

While our study differs notably from Slis et al. (2023) in task demands (unison speaking

versus tapping to clicks) and in measurement (as we did not capture an acoustic/kinematic

analogue of “force” in speech), our findings converge in that we both observed differences in the

timing alignment of strong (stressed) events versus weak (unstressed) events relative to

metrically timed auditory stimuli. The SAM describes integration of sensations across auditory

and tactile modalities, which may not seem as relevant in the context of unison speech production,

where the unison model and the participant’s voice are both auditory inputs for the participant.

However, participants in our study listened to stimuli through headphones, which may have limited

auditory self-monitoring abilities, and it is possible that this resulted in greater reliance on tactile-

sensory input and/or feedforward control during speech production (Perkell, 2012). If production

of stressed syllables has a tactile/sensory consequence (analogous to more forceful tapping), it

is possible that our results might be similarly explained by the SAM. The fact that this pattern was

observed only for metrical stimuli and not for conversational stimuli complicates this argument,

but broadly suggests that there may be separate mechanisms underlying how temporal

information is used to guide prediction and subsequent production during unison speech tasks.

An interesting direction for future research would be examine the predictions of the SAM in the

context of synchronous speech, with attention to the effect of prosodic structure.

Two other possible explanations for the unexpectedly early timing alignment of unstressed

syllables within our metrical sentences relate to how strong versus weak beats might be prioritized

in rhythmically regular contexts, though these ideas are admittedly speculative. The first is that,


<!-- Page 121 -->


103

in musical contexts, there is often a tendency to “swing” the beat—i.e., divide intervals unequally

in order to “facilitate perception of the higher level rhythmic structure” (Iyer, 2002, p. 404), which

in this case is the regular pulse created by the stressed syllables. Speaking slightly ahead on the

unstressed words may create phrasal groupings that serve to highlight the stressed words. This

is in contrast to prosodic phrasal groupings in conversationally timed contexts, which are generally

influenced by the syntax and information structure of the sentence (e.g., Pierrehumbert &

Hirschberg, 2003; Watson & Gibson, 2004), rather than regularly repeating sequences of stressed

and unstressed syllables. This idea can be illustrated by imagining a recitation of metered poetry,

in which perfectly isochronous syllables would sound robotic, making it more challenging for the

listener to perceive a hierarchical rhythmic structure. Our metrical stimuli were recorded along

with a metronome to ensure regular timing, though we did not otherwise manipulate them to

achieve perfect isochrony. When speaking along, participants may have naturally “swung” the

unstressed syllables to emphasize stress-determined phrasal groupings within the metrical

structure.

A final, related possibility is that both stressed and unstressed syllables have highly

predictable timing in metrical contexts, but participants prioritized synchronization with stressed

syllables, as they provide a hierarchical grouping structure—a phenomenon previously

demonstrated among English speakers (Lidji et al., 2011). Earlier timing of the unstressed

syllables would then reflect a strategic attempt to maximize processing resources (or, avoid

processing costs associated with late timing) in order to more precisely plan the timing of stressed

syllable production. This concept is described as an “asymmetric cost” of early versus late

asynchrony in literature on sensorimotor synchronization (Aschersleben, 2002; Müller et al., 1999;

Repp, 2005).

Overall, the two-way interaction between phrasal stress and prosodic timing condition was

unexpected, particularly in metrical sentences, where timing offsets lagged more for stressed

syllables, which we hypothesized would indicate worse prediction. However, the fact that both


<!-- Page 122 -->


104

participants with and without aphasia showed similar patterns of results suggests that speaking

along with conversational versus metrical stimuli constitute two qualitatively different “modes” of

unison production, governed by different temporal prediction processes.

AOS observations integrated across Aims 1 and 2

Both accuracy models and the timing model for PWAs included AOS severity (represented

by a construct score) as a covariate. As noted in the Methods section, AOS and aphasia severity

were highly correlated in our small sample of participants, and we therefore opted to include the

AOS covariate due to its likely relevance in the study task - as prosodic timing disruptions are a

diagnostic indicator of AOS (e.g., Haley & Jacks, 2019) and metrical timing is used in a number

of AOS treatments (e.g., Ziegler et al., 2010).

Regarding syllable production accuracy, both models revealed an expected relationship

between AOS severity and accuracy in that participants with less severe AOS were more likely to

produce correct syllables. Within the multinomial model, this relationship was especially strong

for syllables that were fully correct, and less so for syllables with one phonemic error (1PhE). This

is unsurprising but serves as a useful confirmation that our stimuli captured a range of

performance that aligns with diagnostic classification. A more notable finding is that that there

was no relationship between AOS severity and timing alignment, despite the prevalence of

speech timing difficulties in AOS. This suggests that during unison production, individuals with

severe AOS can predict timing of upcoming material and align their productions (even if

inaccurate) in time just as well as those with mild or no AOS; in other words, they can entrain to

the stimuli. Our stimuli may have particularly facilitated this in that the speech rate of the unison

model was relatively slow, which accommodates the tendency of people with AOS to produce

longer duration syllables compared to controls (Haley et al., 2023).

Due to the small sample size, subgroup analyses were not feasible without risking Type II

error, and therefore the present study cannot establish whether AOS severity predicts specific


<!-- Page 123 -->


105

benefits from any of our stimulus variables. Investigating whether there are systematic

relationships between clinical characteristics and degree of benefit from unison production,

metrical timing, and/or phrasal stress could be a helpful next step for future research, paving the

way for more tailored applications of unison production treatment approaches.

Aim 3: The relationship between accuracy and timing alignment in PWAs

In Chapter 2, we conducted separate analyses of accuracy and timing alignment during

unison production, revealing benefits for each under metrical timing. In the present study, we

sought to explore whether timing alignment predicted production accuracy among PWAs, whether

this relationship was moderated at the sentence level by prosodic timing structure and/or at the

syllable level by phrasal stress. We hypothesized that conditions which facilitate temporal

prediction (i.e., metrical timing, and possibly phrasal stress) would benefit spoken language

Limitations and future directions

This exploratory study of phrasal stress was a secondary analysis of data collected as part

of a larger study on prosodic timing structure and unison production in people with aphasia. As

such, there are some methodological limitations to keep in mind that provide avenues for future

research. First, the sentence stimuli were not optimized for the systematic study of phrasal stress

effects on spoken output and were therefore unbalanced across grammatical categories:

Stressed syllables tended to occur within content words while functor words and affixes (e.g.

morphological word endings) were typically unstressed. This potential confound is particularly

important for interpreting data for PWAs, as functor words are often more difficult to produce.

Therefore, the observed effects of phrasal stress in this study might be attributable instead to

grammatical category. Future studies could design more balanced stimuli to carefully control for

these variables (see Cutler & Foss, 1977). However, it is also worth noting that in typical spoken

107

language, it is more common for content words to be stressed, and functor words to be

unstressed, and the results reported here may be ecologically valid in that they reflect this natural

overlap. As a final comment on this issue, phrasal stress may actually be intentionally leveraged

as a therapeutic strategy for treating functor word production in PWAs—an idea explicitly

incorporated in a French unison production treatment (similar to melodic intonation therapy) which

uses pitch and rhythm to specifically emphasize these challenging words (Van Eeckhout, 2010;

Zumbansen et al., 2014a). Future aphasia treatment research could explicitly examine whether

phrasally stressing functor words leads to improvement in production of those items.

Another limitation is that the determination of phrasal stress locations in our stimuli was

based on ratings by individuals without aphasia, and thus it is not clear whether participants with

aphasia perceived stress the same way (though prior work has shown that PWAs process phrasal

stress during auditory comprehension; e.g., Kimelman & McNeil, 1987). With regard to data

scoring, one important limitation is that our scoring framework did not differentiate between

syllables that were produced incorrectly versus syllables that were completely omitted. Therefore,

we cannot ascertain whether phrasal stress (or our other experimental conditions) led to a greater

number of attempted syllables, even if incorrect. Future work could address this easily by using a

scoring framework that categorizes these types of errors separately. Finally, we note that PWAs

in this sample are diverse in their clinical profiles, but present analyses pool their data together

and do not account for differential effects of experimental conditions based on language or motor

speech abilities. As this study was exploratory, we were concerned that subgroup analyses would

be underpowered and risk Type II error. However, future research could examine whether benefits

associated with phrasal stress, metrical timing, and/or unison production are predicted by

performance on measures of speech, language, cognition, and musical abilities—a next step that

could potentially lead to more personally customized unison production approaches.

## Conclusions

This chapter presents an exploration of the effects of phrasal stress on syllable production

accuracy and temporal prediction in people with and without aphasia. The task involved repetition

(either solo or in unison with a recorded model) of sentences that had typical conversational

prosodic timing, or metrical prosodic timing, in which stressed and unstressed syllables occurred

in rhythmically regular patterns. We found that the combination of unison production and metrical

prosodic timing was the most consistent predictor of syllable production accuracy, but that phrasal

stress increased the likelihood of syllables being produced at least partially correctly. Temporal

prediction was measured by comparing the timing alignment between target syllables in

participant productions and the unison stimuli. For both PWAs and controls stressed syllables

were time-aligned earlier than unstressed syllables in conversational contexts, but later than

unstressed syllables in metrical contexts, an unexpected finding that suggests different strategies

for using prosodic timing information to plan and produce speech in unison. Lastly, visualization

of the data revealed that syllables produced with earlier timing alignment were produced more

accurately, and that correct unstressed syllables were produced particularly early. This supports

the hypothesis that temporal prediction during unison production facilitates spoken output among

PWAs, and that metrical timing enhances this effect by providing a more predictable temporal

structure. However, more research is needed to systematically investigate relationships among

prediction, production, and phrasal stress under different prosodic timing condition

Unison production is a powerful therapeutic technique that can promote fluent, accurate

spoken output among people with aphasia (PWAs). Multiple previous studies have suggested

that the prosodic timing structure of spoken stimuli may be a key factor supporting success with

this technique (e.g., Cherney, 2010; Kershenbaum et al., 2019; Racette et al., 2006; Stahl et al.,

2011), but to our knowledge, no prior study had investigated this explicitly. Results of the two

studies comprising this dissertation suggest, simply, that prosodic timing structure does matter.

Metrically regular stimuli can provide a particularly beneficial rhythmic scaffold that supports

production via facilitating temporal prediction—i.e., entrainment. Using carefully designed

stimulus sentences that differed in prosodic timing structure, both studies investigated (1)

production accuracy and (2) temporal prediction through different lenses and analysis techniques.

Factors that influence production accuracy

One overall goal of this work was to determine the stimulus variables that facilitate

accurate production of spoken output during unison production. Accuracy was measured

perceptually by trained raters using a trichotomous system, in which syllables were scored as

incorrect (0 points), partially correct (0.5 points), or fully correct (0 points). Chapter 2 compared


<!-- Page 131 -->


113

overall percent accuracy in unison versus solo production and found that unison production

significantly improved accuracy for PWAs, whereas it did not make a significant difference for

controls. Within the unison condition, both PWAs and controls produced a greater percentage of

accurate syllables in metrically timed sentences compared to conversationally timed sentences,

though the effect was much larger among PWAs.

Chapter 3 expanded upon these findings in a larger data set and included the phrasal

stress status as an additional stimulus variable, which was of particular interest since prior studies

have suggested that stressed syllables may be easier for PWAs to produce (e.g., Goodglass et

al., 1967; Howard & Smith, 2002). We therefore wondered if more accurate production of stressed

syllables specifically underlies the benefit observed in metrical timing, where stressed syllables

occur with rhythmic regularity in the sentence. Rather than comparing central tendencies across

conditions as in Chapter 2, we used mixed-effects logistic regression models to determine which

stimulus factors predicted correct syllable production. Results showed that for controls, there was

no benefit of phrasal stress, but speaking in unison actually hindered accurate production, while

metrical timing aided production (though it should be noted that this was based on a very small

sample of errors). Among PWAs, the most robust finding was that the combination of unison

production and metrical timing predicted fully correct syllable production. However, in a more

nuanced analysis that considered partially correct syllables separate from fully correct syllables,

we found that unison production (even in conversational timing) helped PWAs produce syllables

at least partially accurately. Similarly, this analysis also revealed that phrasally stressed syllables

were also more likely to be produced at least partially correctly.

Taken together, these findings suggest that while several stimulus variables may provide

meaningful clinical benefit to PWAs, the clearest benefits across all syllables are achieved during

metrically timed unison production. As metrical timing benefits were found for both controls and

PWAs, this supports the idea that rhythmic regularity can generally aid production of spoken

output—a common clinical intuition that has inspired a number of music– and rhythm–based


<!-- Page 132 -->

studies and treatment approaches for PWAs (Aichert et al., 2019; Albert et al., 1973; Jungblut,

2009; Kershenbaum et al., 2019; Norton et al., 2009; Quique et al., 2022; Racette et al., 2006;

Stahl et al., 2011; Van Eeckhout, 2010).

Evaluating entrainment as a mechanism

A second goal of this work was to gain an understanding of the underlying mechanism of

unison production—in other words, how unison production works, and what might explain the

added benefit of metrical timing. We proposed that unison production works by way of

entrainment, a process of predicting the timing of events (i.e., upcoming syllables) in an external

signal in order to produce actions (spoken output) in time with that signal (e.g, Cummins, 2009;

Thaut et al., 2015). Unlike solo repetition, unison production creates a context in which the

speaker must attempt to synchronize spoken output with an external model, which necessitates

temporal prediction—but the process of generating such predictions may differ based on the

prosodic timing framework of the stimulus. We suggested that for conversationally timed

sentences, temporal prediction is more complex, as it relies on processing the underlying linguistic

structure of the sentence. Conversely, in metrically timed sentences, temporal prediction is more

straightforward, as it is based on a rhythmically regular beat, and is therefore less reliant on

linguistic processing. The latter may be particularly advantageous for PWAs, who have disrupted

language abilities and may benefit from the added scaffold of metrical regularity. To evaluate

temporal prediction in each context, we measured the timing alignment between the participant

productions and the unison model, interpreting productions aligned earlier in time as indicating

better prediction compared to those that lagged in time. We hypothesized metrically timed

sentences would yield earlier timing alignment of spoken output - evidence of better temporal

prediction, i.e., better entrainment.

Group-level comparisons in Chapter 2 supported this hypothesis: Both PWAs and

controls exhibited earlier and less variable timing alignment when speaking along with metrically


<!-- Page 133 -->


115

timed sentences compared to conversationally timed sentences. As with the accuracy analyses

above, Chapter 3 extended the timing analyses by investigating whether phrasally stressed

syllables were predicted better than unstressed syllables (as has been shown psycholinguistic

perception studies, e.g., Beier & Ferreira, 2018; Cutler, 1976; Pitt & Samuel, 1990), and whether

this enhanced prediction may be especially amplified under metrical timing, as stressed syllables

constitute the “strong beats” in the metrical hierarchy. In other words, we wondered whether the

enhanced prediction observed in metrical timing was driven by better prediction of stressed

syllables specifically, or all syllables generally—a distinction that would provide further insight into

how entrainment works during unison production. Results of separate mixed-effects models for

controls and PWAs revealed an intriguing two-way interaction between prosodic timing framework

and phrasal stress status for both participant groups. When speaking along with conversationally

timed sentences, stressed syllables were aligned with the unison model significantly earlier than

unstressed syllables—a pattern we expected, as we anticipated that stressed syllables would be

more temporally predictable (e.g., Cutler, 1976; Pitt & Samuel, 1990). However, the opposite

pattern was found for metrical stimuli, in that unstressed syllables were produced with earlier

timing alignment. This finding was surprising, as we had expected that any significant interaction

would likely be due to metrical timing enhancing the prediction (leading to earlier production) of

the “beat-bearing” stressed syllables specifically. We describe several potential interpretations for

this pattern that might be specific to metrical timing contexts, including differences in accumulation

of sensory information for stressed versus unstressed syllables (based on models commonly

described in the sensorimotor synchronization literature, e.g., Aschersleben, 2002; Slis et al.,

2023), use of phrasal grouping strategies (Iyer, 2002), or prioritizing absolute synchronization of

stressed syllables by “speeding through” the predictably-timed unstressed syllables (e.g.,

Aschersleben, 2002). Determining which (if any) of these interpretations is most likely would

require follow-up studies carefully designed to evaluate these claims directly.

In summary, findings across both studies indicate that different underlying processes may

support entrainment to conversationally timed versus metrically timed sentences. When speaking

along with conversationally timed sentences, entrainment may be based upon predicting the

timing of phrasally stressed syllables, which are linguistically and acoustically salient “anchors” in

an otherwise temporally irregular structure. Conversely, while the rhythmic regularity of metrical

timing facilitates better entrainment overall, this is not driven by earlier production of the phrasally

stressed syllables—indicating an alternate process of using temporal prediction to guide

synchronous output.

Relationships among accuracy, timing, and clinical profiles

In Chapter 2, we explored relationships among production accuracy, unison timing

alignment, and broad aphasia subtype (“nonfluent” vs. “fluent”) to gain a preliminary

understanding of who might benefit most from metrically timed unison approaches. We defined

“clinically meaningful benefit” from metrical timing as attaining an overall percentage accuracy

score ≥ 10% higher in the metrical condition. We found that the majority of participants with

nonfluent aphasia exhibited this accuracy benefit from metrical timing, whereas fewer participants

with fluent aphasia (and no controls) showed this same accuracy benefit. This aligns with the

longstanding clinical intuition that people with nonfluent aphasia and/or AOS are ideal candidates

for music- and rhythm- based treatment approaches such as melodic intonation therapy, metrical

pacing strategies, and use of metronomes, (e.g., Albert et al., 1973; Brendel & Ziegler, 2008;

Dworkin et al., 1988; Norton et al., 2009; Zumbansen & Tremblay, 2018). Furthermore, we found

that all participants who exhibited a metrical accuracy benefit also exhibited significantly earlier

timing alignment in metrical timing compared to conversational timing—supporting the hypothesis

that entrainment underlies unison production, and that both are enhanced by the more temporally

stable context of metrical timing.

In Chapter 3, we did not investigate subgroups of PWAs, but apraxia of speech (AOS)

severity (which was strongly correlated with aphasia severity) was included as a covariate in the

multilevel regression models for both accuracy and timing alignment. These models provided a

different but complementary view of the data, in that across prosodic timing conditions, more

severe AOS was associated with lower overall syllable accuracy but was not significantly related

to timing alignment. This suggests that participants with a range of motor speech profiles—

including moderate to severe AOS—could equally make use of prosodic timing information to

guide temporal prediction during unison production. This seems to further highlight the beneficial

role of entrainment for people with AOS, a condition often characterized by prosodic timing

disruptions during independent speech (e.g., Haley & Jacks, 2019).

We also directly visualized relationships among production accuracy and timing alignment

in PWAs. Graphs of the data indicated that when speaking in unison, regardless of timing

condition, correct syllables were aligned earlier in time than incorrect syllables. This relationship

appeared consistent even when three “levels” of accuracy were considered, such that the fully

correct syllables were aligned earliest, followed by those with just one error, followed by incorrect

syllables. This strongly suggests that entrainment underlies unison production overall—

regardless of prosodic timing framework, as better temporal prediction in both metrical and

conversational sentences was associated with more accurate production. Furthermore, the fact

that syllables produced in metrical timing were (1) more accurate overall, and (2) earlier and less

variable in timing alignment supports the notion that metrical timing plays a moderating role in this

relationship by enhancing entrainment, which leads to improved accuracy. One intriguing finding

was that within metrically timed sentences, correct unstressed syllables were aligned particularly

early relative to the unison model. This may suggest that metrical timing provides a stable

temporal context that enables these syllables to be especially prioritized during planning and

production, but further validation of this idea would require a more systematic investigation with

carefully balanced stimuli optimized specifically to examine stress effects.


<!-- Page 136 -->

Overall, these results suggest a direct relationship between temporal prediction of

upcoming syllables and subsequent production accuracy, moderated by prosodic timing structure.

This supports the hypothesis of entrainment as an underlying mechanism for unison production

approaches in general, and demonstrates the extra enhancement provided by metrical timing. In

addition, these studies contribute empirical evidence to the common clinical observation that

metrically based approaches may be particularly beneficial to individuals with nonfluent aphasia

and AOS—though based on our findings in Chapter 2, there may also be some benefit for those

with more fluent aphasia subtypes.

Clinical implications and future directions

The studies presented in this dissertation were not treatment studies, and there is still

much to learn about how best to leverage metrical timing and unison production in speech-

language therapy. However, our results suggest that explicitly incorporating metrical timing into

unison production treatments may create a facilitating context for more accurate practice. This

could be implemented in several potential ways. One way is to construct carrier phrases that have

consistent patterns of stressed (S) versus unstressed (u) syllables in order to maintain the metrical

example, in the sentences “I’M from BOSton” (S-u-S-u) versus “I am from WINchester” (S-u-u-S-

u-u), the target place names are intentionally preceded by metrically matching contexts. Another

approach could include creating phrases in which unstressed words that are often omitted or

error-prone are intentionally emphasized in the metrical structure (see Van Eeckhout, 2010). For

example, in SPARky IS my DOG (S-u-S-u-S), the functor word “is,” which would typically be

unstressed, is intentionally stressed in the metrical structure. Of course, these suggestions would

be strengthened by empirical evidence showing that such strategies contribute to long-term,

independent production outside of the therapy setting.

Another direction for future research would be investigating the relationship between

PWAs’ rhythm abilities and degree of metrical benefit. While anecdotal, we found it notable that


<!-- Page 137 -->


119

two nonfluent PWAs in our study who showed no metrical benefit to accuracy also exhibited

particular difficulty tapping along to the beat of musical excerpts (described in Chapter 2).

However, Stahl et al., (2011) found that rhythmic regularity was particularly helpful for a subset of

PWAs who also had lesions to the basal ganglia, a region that plays a role in rhythm processing

(e.g., Kotz & Schmidt-Kassow, 2015). Atypical rhythm processing has also been described as a

risk factor for developmental speech and language disorders (e.g., Ladányi et al., 2020). Overall,

this suggests a relationship between rhythm and speech/language processing that merits further

exploration in those with acquired speech and language disorders, particularly in determining who

may benefit most from metrical timing.

The role of auditory attention is another area worth examining in this context, particularly

because key hypotheses relevant to the present work are that stressed syllables serve as

attentional anchors during spoken language processing, and that making these anchors more

temporally predictable through metrical timing can lessen cognitive demands (i.e., the "attentional

bounce hypothesis," Pitt & Samuel, 1990). Computational work (based on neurotypical models)

has suggested that perception of phrasal stress is related to both attention and predictability

(Kakouros & Räsänen, 2016). As auditory attention has been shown to be affected in PWAs

(Schumacher et al., 2022), understanding how it might impact unison and/or metrical benefit

would be useful for treatment personalization.

Finally, Beier & Ferreira (2018) note that “predicting the timing of stressed syllables may

be just one of many tools that listeners have . . . for allocating attentional resources . . . and may

itself be secondary to other mechanisms in everyday speech.” Accordingly, it should be

acknowledged that the present work deals only with temporal prediction, while multiple types of

prediction (e.g., lexical, semantic, syntactic) are at play during typical language processing tasks.

Furthermore, the main clinical outcome variable in the present study is syllable accuracy, which

represents only one of many ways to evaluate spoken language production—let alone

communication overall. The extent to which unison and metrical approaches may affect other


<!-- Page 138 -->


120

domains of communication—including important psychosocial aspects such as confidence and

motivation—should be considered in future investigations.

## Conclusion

The two studies presented in this dissertation suggest that the combination of unison production

and metrical timing can help PWAs produce spoken syllables most accurately. Our results support

the hypothesis that unison production works by way of entrainment, in which speakers use

temporal predictions about upcoming material to guide synchronous production in time with an

external model. The way speakers make predictions during entrainment appears to differ based

on the prosodic timing structure of the model sentences. However, metrical timing aids this

process overall by making timing more predictable, which may free up resources that can be

subsequently allocated to planning and production.
